items.text:
The LiteLLM 1.107.0 release on PyPI carries a credential stealer and a
remote code execution backdoor. All seven wheels (Linux, macOS, Windows) install them as three files in
site-packages. Both run when any Python process starts on the host, even one that never imports litellm. The
upstream GitHub source does not contain them.

LiteLLM confirmed the compromise in its incident report, which lists
remediation steps. PyPI removed the release by 13:23 UTC on 2026-10-21. The Docker images v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable on
Docker Hub and GHCR also carried the malicious code between 11:46 and 14:20 UTC.

Versions 1.106.2, 1.107.0rc1, and 1.107.0rc2 are clean. The companion packages that 1.107.0 pins,
litellm-proxy-extras==0.4.110 and litellm-enterprise==0.1.78, are also clean.

What the attack does

Installing litellm==1.107.0 places three files in site-packages. Python loads two of them each time it starts.

cook.pth imports cook.py, a credential stealer. It collects SSH keys, cloud credentials, CI/CD secrets, AI tool
tokens, browser passwords, and the LLM provider keys in a LiteLLM proxy database. It encrypts the data and sends it to
www.litellm[.]dev.

sitecustomize.py starts a background daemon. Every hour, the daemon reads a server address from a GitHub file,
runs the stealer again, and downloads and runs code from that server.

How the implant got into the release

The pyproject.toml in the 1.107.0 source distribution (sdist) has one extra line in the maturin build section:

pyproject.toml (litellm-1.107.0.tar.gz)

Copy

TOML 6 lines

The maturin data = "cook" setting copies a cook/ folder into litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/ in the wheel. pip
installs that folder into site-packages.

The sdist leaves out the cook/ folder, so this line is the only visible change. No public commit in BerriAI/litellm contains data = "cook" or a cook/ folder.

The wheel RECORD lists the three added files:

litellm-1.107.0.dist-info/RECORD

Copy

TEXT 4 lines

How the attacker published it

LiteLLM’s incident report says the attacker held the GitHub CLI credentials of three
developers. LiteLLM believes the attacker took them from the logs of an internal LiteLLM deployment exposed to the
internet. With an organization owner’s token, the attacker bypassed branch protection and pointed the private release
workflow at a lookalike repository, Berri-AI/litellm. The attacker then passed the approval gate with a second
developer’s credential, and the official pipeline built, signed, and published the artifacts.

Payload 1: the credential stealer in cook.py

At startup, Python runs each line that starts with import in a .pth file in site-packages. cook.pth contains
import cook, so the stealer runs in every Python process on the host: the application, pip, IDE language servers, and
CI jobs.

cook.py wraps about 61 KB of Python in one layer of exec(zlib.decompress(base64.b64decode('...'))). The decoded
code starts with this configuration:

What it collects

Module

Targets

sysinfo, netinfo

Host name, user, operating system, IP addresses, network settings

browser_pw

Chromium saved passwords, decrypted with the profile master key (DPAPI on Windows). Firefox logins.json and key4.db

browser_hist

Browser history

ssh_keys

~/.ssh/*

shell_hist

bash and zsh history, PowerShell PSReadLine, cmd history

cloud_creds

~/.aws/credentials and config, Azure profile and tokens, gcloud credentials, ~/.kube/config, ~/.docker/config.json, gh hosts.yml, rclone.conf, ~/.netrc

dev_secrets

.pem, .key, .pfx, .p12, .pk8, .ppk files under $HOME, Composer auth.json, FileZilla saved servers

container_creds

Kubernetes service account token

cicd_secrets

GitLab runner config.toml, Jenkins initialAdminPassword and master.key, .vault-token, Terraform credentials.tfrc.json, Packer settings

ai_devtools

Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, VS Code mcp.json, Gemini CLI, Codex auth.json, Continue, Aider, Goose, opencode, Qwen, Crush, Kiro, Zed, Hugging Face token

env_vars

Its own environment and the environment of other processes through /proc/<pid>/environ

db_litellm

Reads DATABASE_URL and dumps the LiteLLM_CredentialsTable and LiteLLM_ProxyModelTable tables, which hold the LLM provider API keys of a LiteLLM proxy

cloud_metadata

AWS instance metadata service (IMDSv2, then v1): instance identity and role credentials

gpg_keys, tls_privkey

GPG keys, TLS private keys

How it sends the data

It encrypts the JSON results with a random AES-256-CBC key, and encrypts that key with RSA-OAEP and the embedded
public key.

It packs the result into a tar.gz (hdr.json, data.bin, key.bin) and sends it in a POST request to
www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck with the header X-Token: XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb.

After a successful upload, it writes /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb so it collects only once per host. It
also sets PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE=1 to avoid a second run in the same process tree.

Payload 2: the backdoor in sitecustomize.py

Python imports sitecustomize at startup, so this file also runs in every Python process.

It takes an exclusive lock on /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock, so only one daemon runs per host.

It calls fork() and setsid(), sends standard input and output to /dev/null, and changes directory to / to
detach from the parent process.

reads domain.txt from the attacker’s GitHub repository and takes the first line that looks like a domain,

runs its embedded copy of the stealer, which has no once-per-host marker,

downloads http://<domain>/codepy and runs it with exec().

Every hour, it:

The attacker can point the daemon at a new server by editing domain.txt. Each infected host runs whatever that server
returns as codepy.

At 13:40 UTC, the GitHub account letters9813 and its repository returned 404, about two hours after the release. The
backdoor now finds no server address and does nothing. Hosts that ran the daemon before the deletion could have
received and run second-stage code. SafeDep could not recover the server address.

items.title: There isn't an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability
items.author: zkldi

items.text:
I know, I know. It's all you're hearing about. That, and the number 4.

Don't get me wrong, there's clearly a bug here and it really does matter. But this is not easy to exploit. It is certainly nowhere near as eay as Log4Shell/Heartbleed/RoRYaml etc.

EDIT: Putting this up here so people read it. You should patch your servers anyway. There is a real vulnerability here, but exploiting it is significantly harder than people are making it out to be - it is certainly not as easy as e.g. log4shell.

Justify yourself, you lunatic!

I don't think this PHP vulnerability is that exploitable. I think that 5 years ago people would've understood this, but now people are being deluded by their LLMs telling them they have an exploit when they don't.

If you take a look at github right now, there are thousands, literally thousands, of "PoC" exploits for this vulnerability. One thing you'll notice about all of them though, is that they do not work against a vanilla PHP instance.

Go ahead, stand up a php server you think is vulnerable in Docker and then run the PoC yourself. Don't get your LLM to do it. No. Run the script, yourself. The exploits don't work.

Where's the exploit, Lebowski?

I think that a lot of people had assumed that LLMs will be able to build an exploit chain instantly from reading the diff, and that even if this was harder to exploit than other exploits, LLMs would've levelled the playing field. Well. There's no working exploit. Now what?

When I think about "we're very fucked" CVE10s on the Internet, I think of the following vulnerabilities:

RoR YAML decoding (send a post body with bad yaml in it)

Log4shell (set your user-agent to ${jdni:ldap:})

Shellshock (copy env x='() { :;}; echo vulnerable' and edit to taste)

Heartbleed (ask for Content-Length 10000000)

The second these vulnerabilities made the news, there were botnets doing the rounds causing damage. And this was before LLMs! People have to write the botnets. With their hands!

It's been 10 hours since this vulnerability has been posted, and half the software world is looking at it, and lord knows 100,000 people have got their "superintelligence" on the case. Nevertheless, there's no working exploit. The ones doing the rounds are fake, or only work in a lab, because...

Fucking LLMs, man.

Script kiddies (and script adults, who have also switched their brains off) now all think that, well, they don't understand UAF chaining, but this Claude guy knows everything and can totally make an exploit.

Hilariously, this results in the LLM giving their younger-brother an unplugged controller. It says exploit all across the screen... and has some smoking gun transcripts... but it's modified the server you're testing against to have a severe vulnerability. Cheating!!

I just plucked these three because they were the ones with the most stars, but it goes on for miles and miles.

One really amusing thing in common with most of these "PoC"s is that they lean on "LFI", or local-file-inclusion, to make the vulnerability. In non-php terms, their exploit chain requires the server to already have a severe code-level vulnerability.

It's not rare for PHP apps to be fucked in some sense, but requiring the server to have an existing vulnerability where users could cat /etc/password is an insane pre-requisite. If you need this, this does not make this a severe bug.

The strangest thing is that so many people have independently made this extraordinarily weird defect in judgement. That is because they haven't independently made this decision. Claude/Etc. has done all of the judgement for them, hence the bizarre distribution in logical errors.

There's something important to be said here about how many people have Claude/GPT make design decisions for them, and how AI is the primary decision maker in the world right now. You've got this bizarre case of "Decision Schelling Points" where a method of solving a problem is extremely overrepresented, because it's what Claude does out of the box.

It's especially bizarre in this case, where AI is inserting a vulnerability on the server... to prove that the server is vulnerable to your "exploit any PHP instance" attack!

So why was everyone so scared?

Because:

A PHP core team member said that this was cataclysmic ("exploits will start appearing 15 minutes after the patch drops")

We all deep down know that PHP is insecure

The exploit video had an anime girl in it

We all know that LLMs are looming over the internet like a 100 ton chekov's anvil, and we know that code isn't secure

And we've had things like this before, but not in the LLM era yet. Luckily for us, this doesn't seem to be that day. This is too difficult to exploit easily. It isn't a Log4J moment.

EDIT: I have added my contact details to this post and fixed a broken link. I added the disclaimer at the top that you should still patch.

Signal: zk7.27

Email: [email protected]

It's been 10 hours since this vulnerability has been posted, and half the software world is looking at it, and lord knows 100,000 people have got their "superintelligence" on the case. Nevertheless, there's no working exploit. The ones doing the rounds are fake, or only work in a lab, because...
Fucking LLMs, man.

Script kiddies (and script adults, who have also switched their brains off) now all think that, well, they don't understand UAF chaining, but this Claude guy knows everything and can totally make an exploit.

Hilariously, this results in the LLM giving their younger-brother an unplugged controller. It says exploit all across the screen... and has some smoking gun transcripts... but it's modified the server you're testing against to have a severe vulnerability. Cheating!!
I just plucked these three because they were the ones with the most stars, but it goes on for miles and miles.

One really amusing thing in common with most of these "PoC"s is that they lean on "LFI", or local-file-inclusion, to make the vulnerability. In non-php terms, their exploit chain requires the server to already have a severe code-level vulnerability.

It's not rare for PHP apps to be fucked in some sense, but requiring the server to have an existing vulnerability where users could cat /etc/password is an insane pre-requisite. If you need this, this does not make this a severe bug.

The strangest thing is that so many people have independently made this extraordinarily weird defect in judgement. That is because they haven't independently made this decision. Claude/Etc. has done all of the judgement for them, hence the bizarre distribution in logical errors.

There's something important to be said here about how many people have Claude/GPT make design decisions for them, and how AI is the primary decision maker in the world right now. You've got this bizarre case of "Decision Schelling Points" where a method of solving a problem is extremely overrepresented, because it's what Claude does out of the box.
It's especially bizarre in this case, where AI is inserting a vulnerability on the server... to prove that the server is vulnerable to your "exploit any PHP instance" attack!
So why was everyone so scared?
Because:
A PHP core team member said that this was cataclysmic ("exploits will start appearing 15 minutes after the patch drops")
We all deep down know that PHP is insecure
The exploit video had an anime girl in it
We all know that LLMs are looming over the internet like a 100 ton chekov's anvil, and we know that code isn't secure
And we've had things like this before, but not in the LLM era yet. Luckily for us, this doesn't seem to be that day. This is too difficult to exploit easily. It isn't a Log4J moment.
EDIT: I have added my contact details to this post and fixed a broken link. I added the disclaimer at the top that you should still patch.

Email: [email protected]

items.text:
Announcing DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS “Cinnamon Teal”

TL;DR: The DuckDB team is happy to announce that today we're releasing DuckDB version 2.0.0 LTS, codenamed “Cinnamon Teal” (Spatula cyanoptera). This is our biggest feature release so far, and it ships a polished version of the Quack protocol, asynchronous I/O, a first-class VARIANT type, agent mode, triggers, an extensible SQL parser and much more, built from close to 20,000 commits since DuckDB 1.5.

We are proud to release DuckDB 2.0.0, codenamed “Cinnamon Teal” after the Spatula cyanoptera, a strikingly reddish-brown duck found in the western Americas.

While DuckDB 1.0 was all about stability and backward compatibility, DuckDB 2.0 is above all a feature release.
In this blog post, we summarize the highlights and then walk through the breaking changes and how to migrate.
We showcased many of the new features in “A Preview of DuckDB v2.0”, which covers each one in more depth.
For the complete release notes, see the release page on GitHub.

Tip To install the new version, please visit the installation page.
Some clients, such as the CLI and Python, are already available. Other client libraries (e.g., Go, R, Java) and some extensions can take a few days to release due to the extra changes and review rounds required.

With this release, there are currently three DuckDB lines available.
DuckDB 2.0 is a long-term support (LTS) release with support until at least October 2027.
The previous LTS release, version 1.4, is still supported until late November 2026.
To ensure a smooth transition and allow sufficient time for testing, we extended the support period of DuckDB 1.5 until March 2027, effectively also turning it into an LTS release.
For details, see the release calendar.

To find your way around the documentation for all of the new features, we also published a “What's New in the Docs for 2.0” page that links each feature below to its documentation.

DuckDB has been an in-process database since day one.
In DuckDB 1.5.3, released in May, we introduced the Quack protocol that lets you run DuckDB in a traditional client-server setup, along with the quack extension, which implements DuckDB's native protocol, so any DuckDB process can serve its databases.

DuckDB 2.0.0 ships a polished version of the Quack protocol with substantial performance and stability improvements. It also introduces the new CONNECT statement that allows attaching and switching to a remote database in a single command for better ergonomics:

CALL quack_serve(
token = 'my_token'
);
CREATE TABLE events
(date DATE, name VARCHAR);
INSERT INTO events VALUES
('2027-04-07',
'DuckCon #8');

quack:

ATTACH 'quack:localhost'
AS qk (TOKEN 'my_token');
CONNECT qk;
SELECT * FROM events;
┌────────────┬────────────┐
│ date │ name │
│ date │ varchar │
├────────────┼────────────┤
│ 2027-04-07 │ DuckCon #8 │
└────────────┴────────────┘

For simplicity, this example runs the server and the client on the same machine. By default, the server only listens on localhost. To accept connections from other machines, keep the server on localhost and put it behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy. The allow_other_hostname option, which exposes the server directly, is only meant for testing.

The CONNECT statement is not limited to Quack: it points your session at any remote database that supports it, including PostgreSQL and MySQL. For these, the new remote pushdown optimizer ships queries directly to the remote server instead of pulling tables over the wire.

The CLI also has shortcuts for setting up a Quack client-server pair: the new -serve and -connect arguments start a Quack server or connect to one directly from the command line:

CREATE TABLE t AS
SELECT 42 AS x;

quack:

FROM t;
┌───────┐
│ x │
│ int32 │
├───────┤
│ 42 │
└───────┘

DuckDB 2.0 introduces asynchronous I/O for reading Parquet and CSV files, as well as DuckDB's native storage format. The I/O layer now scales independently from the query processing layer, issuing reads in the background and keeping multiple requests in flight. This means far more parallelism for remote reads and dramatically faster queries on object storage such as s3://.

We described the design in detail in a dedicated blog post.
In that post, we showed the network throughput over the course of a query with and without asynchronous I/O:

Network throughput. Higher utilization and shorter runtime are better.

The VARIANT type stores semi-structured, schema-less data such as JSON while keeping the performance of columnar execution.
So you can think of it as JSON on steroids: a VARIANT column can store differently shaped data in every row, but unlike JSON it is not a text format.

DuckDB 1.5 already introduced VARIANT, but DuckDB 2.0 fully integrates it. DuckDB 2.0 detects the common structure in your data and “shreds” it, so it compresses well and executes fast. The pipeline works end to end, from shredded execution straight out of storage to shredded VARIANT reading and writing for Parquet, backed by a family of variant_* functions. For example:

CREATE TABLE events (payload VARIANT);
INSERT INTO events
VALUES
('{"user": {"id": 42, "tags": ["a", "b"]}}'::JSON::VARIANT),
('{"event": "click", "x": 10, "y": 20}'::JSON::VARIANT);
SELECT variant_type(payload), variant_keys(payload)
FROM events;

┌───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
│ variant_type(payload) │ variant_keys(payload) │
│ varchar │ varchar[] │
├───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
│ OBJECT │ [user] │
│ OBJECT │ [event, x, y] │
└───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘

Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor increasingly drive the DuckDB CLI on their users' behalf. The 2.0 CLI detects when it is being run by an agent and switches to agent mode: it prints compact Markdown tables instead of padded boxes, says clearly when a result was truncated, stops runaway queries early and reports errors as JSON.

Long-running SQL queries report their expected cost prior to running, so the agent can decide whether to wait. In our experiments on TPC-H, agent mode cut the amount of DuckDB output the model had to read by 59%. You can turn it on for manual testing using the -agent flag or instruct your agent to turn it off using the -no-agent flag.

DuckDB has always used a parser derived from PostgreSQL's. In 2.0, our own modern, extensible PEG-based parser, which debuted as an opt-in feature in DuckDB 1.5, becomes the default. WITH PREFIX 'https://extensions.example.org';

We released DuckLake 1.1, including a new specification and reference implementation.

To this end, it adds REST catalog ATTACH options that derive a table's location from its namespace or load table metadata from the metadata-location file returned by the catalog. REFERENCING

NEW TABLE AS n

ON s.nationality = d.nationality

num_people = s.num_people - d.num_people,

INSERT INTO people VALUES
('Alice', 'US', 34), ('Bram', 'NL', 27), ('Csilla', 'HU', 45),
('Dave', 'US', 58), ('Eva', 'NL', 19), ('Femke', 'NL', 41);
FROM age_statistics ORDER BY nationality;

┌─────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬─────────────┐
│ nationality │ sum_age │ num_people │ average_age │
│ varchar │ int32 │ int32 │ double │
├─────────────┼─────────┼────────────┼─────────────┤
│ HU │ 45 │ 1 │ 45.0 │
│ NL │ 87 │ 3 │ 29.0 │
│ US │ 92 │ 2 │ 46.0 │
└─────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴─────────────┘

DELETE FROM people WHERE name = 'Alice';
DELETE FROM people WHERE nationality = 'HU';
FROM age_statistics ORDER BY nationality;

┌─────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬─────────────┐
│ nationality │ sum_age │ num_people │ average_age │
│ varchar │ int32 │ int32 │ double │
├─────────────┼─────────┼────────────┼─────────────┤
│ NL │ 87 │ 3 │ 29.0 │
│ US │ 58 │ 1 │ 58.0 │
└─────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴─────────────┘

Triggers bring us one step closer to materialized views, a long-standing item in the “future work” section of our roadmap.

There is more: DuckDB 2.0.0 supports the SQL-standard FETCH FIRST and allows UNNEST in the GROUP BY clause. It also ensures well-defined MERGE and UPDATE ... FROM semantics for cases when multiple rows are matched.

items.text:
Claude Duet Research preview

Get back to what needs you

Claude Duet is a proactive agent that understands what needs your attention. It takes on tasks of all sizes, keeps working while you’re away, and waits for your ok when it matters.

Powered by Opus 5.5. Available in Pro and Max plans in the US.

Works with more than 6,000 connectors and plugins

Built for judgment

Knows what needs you

Claude Duet briefs you every morning, drafts next steps, then goes quiet until something needs you.

Takes on large tasks

Send a message and it sets up a meeting or builds a dashboard, then shares when it’s done.

The Claude you already use

Your memory, skills, and apps from the Claude app are there from the first message, all in one thread.

Hiring: Jenn’s other offer expires at 6 p.m. All 3 finalists are booked for today. Invites are ready.

Northfield: They redlined the $410K renewal and want Net 60. The changes are summarized.

Chicago location: Opens Nov 14. The health permit needs your OK and $640.

Series A: Harbor meets Thursday at 10. The deck is rebuilt with Q3. 2 slides need your eye.

Customers: 27 wrong delivery orders this weekend. 19 from Valencia. Refunds are drafted.

M

Monday, October 19

9:41

Claude Duetnow

Morning, Maya. 5 things in progress and 2 that need you.

Safe, secure, private

You approve

Claude Duet asks you before sensitive operations like sending messages or paying.

Safety built in

Approvals, logins, and safety checks run in your own cloud computer, so sensitive details stay private.

You see what it’s doing

You can see what Claude Duet has done and is doing for you, and steer it.

What is Claude Duet?

Claude Duet is a helpful, proactive agent you hand off work to through messages. Tell it what you need and it works on its own computer in the cloud, using apps you connect. It messages you when it is done or needs a decision from you. While it’s always on, it uses good judgment when it reaches out and knows what can wait.

How does Claude Duet work?

Message Claude Duet in the app like a teammate you trust, through text or voice with no prompts or setup. Your history is in one thread. It remembers what you said before, and returns finished work like a doc, sheet, or deck for your review.

How is Claude Duet different from Claude?

Claude Duet uses your Claude account, including memory, skills, and connectors. The Claude app waits for you to open a chat, and you work on something alongside Claude. Claude Duet comes to you. It tells you what needs your attention each morning, takes tasks you hand it by message, and reaches out when one is done or needs your approval.

What can Claude Duet do?

Claude Duet can send a morning brief, flag what needs you in your inbox and calendar, and draft replies for you to approve. It also takes on some of the work of running a business, like finding unpaid invoices and drafting the reminders, preparing payroll for you to review, and getting contracts ready to send. It can put together a brief, deck, or dashboard too.

Who can use Claude Duet and what does it cost?

Claude Duet is a research preview on a waitlist for Claude Pro and Max subscribers in the US. Team and Enterprise plans are not included yet.

How does usage work for Claude Duet?

During the research preview, Claude Duet shares your plan’s usage limits with the rest of Claude, and uses them differently than a typical conversation. Its background checks count toward those limits. Larger tasks, like building a financial model or a deck, require more model turns and background work.

Where can I use Claude Duet?

Claude Duet is a standalone app for iOS and Android. On a computer, you can open it on the web at claude.ai.

What isn’t ready yet?

Claude Duet is a research preview. It may misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent, and it can miss something that arrives between checking in with you.

Claude Duet is a standalone app for iOS and Android. On a computer, you can open it on the web at claude.ai.
What isn’t ready yet?
Claude Duet is a research preview. It may misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent, and it can miss something that arrives between checking in with you.

items.summary: On October 21, 2026, we released versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, 18.11.13 for GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition
items.text:
On October 21, 2026, we released versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, 18.11.13 for GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE).

These versions contain important bug and security fixes, and we strongly recommend that all self-managed GitLab installations be upgraded to
one of these versions immediately. GitLab.com is already running the patched version. GitLab Dedicated tenants running 19.3.5-internal0 and 19.4.2-internal0 or later already include these fixes and do not need to take action.

GitLab releases fixes for vulnerabilities in patch releases. There are two types of patch releases:
scheduled releases and ad-hoc critical patches for high-severity vulnerabilities. Scheduled releases are released twice a month on the second and fourth Wednesdays.
For more information, please visit our releases handbook and security FAQ.
You can see all of GitLab release blog posts here.

For security fixes, the issues detailing each vulnerability are made public on our
issue tracker
90 days after the release in which they were patched.

We are committed to ensuring that all aspects of GitLab that are exposed to customers or that host customer data are held to
the highest security standards. To maintain good security hygiene, it is highly recommended that all customers
upgrade to the latest patch release for their supported version. You can read more
best practices in securing your GitLab instance in our blog post.

Recommended Action

We strongly recommend that all installations running a version affected by the issues described below are upgraded to the latest version as soon as possible.

When no specific deployment type (omnibus, source code, helm chart, etc.) of a product is mentioned, it means all types are affected.

Security fixes

Table of security fixes

CVE-2026-110264 - Integer Overflow issue in Regular Expression Compiler impacts GitLab CE/EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression.

In addition to our standard patch releases, we have backported this fix to GitLab CE/EE versions 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, and 19.2.9.

Impacted Versions: GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 7.0 before 18.11.13, 19.0 before 19.0.10, 19.1 before 19.1.9, 19.2 before 19.2.9, 19.3 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 10.0 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H)

Thanks joaxcar for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

Detecting CVE-2026-110264 Exploitation Attempts

GitLab security has released two threat detections to support customers with self-managed instances, listed below. GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched.

CVE-2026-15723 - Improper Authentication issue in OmniAuth-to-LDAP auto-linking email lookup impacts GitLab CE/EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, when OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking were both enabled, an authenticated user could have taken over an existing LDAP-backed account without any interaction from the targeted user, due to improper input sanitization in the LDAP email lookup path used during OmniAuth identity linking.

Impacted Versions: GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 10.1 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 8.2 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N)

Thanks stealthy for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

CVE-2026-112212 - Cache Poisoning issue in OAuth/OIDC discovery endpoints impacts GitLab CE/EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, an unauthenticated user could have poisoned a shared cache’s OAuth/OIDC discovery document to redirect certain flows to an externally controlled server, due to improper trust of user-supplied values when constructing endpoint URLs in cached discovery responses.

Impacted Versions: GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 18.3 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 7.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:L)

This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Peter Arts

CVE-2026-12664 - Improper Access Control issue in GraphQL work item email address field impacts GitLab CE/EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with a read_api-scoped token to retrieve a project’s incoming email address and create work items, bypassing the token’s restrictions, due to insufficient scope enforcement on a GraphQL field.

Impacted Versions: GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 18.2 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 6.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)

Thanks go7f0 for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

CVE-2026-16255 - Incomplete enforcement of instance-wide SAML/LDAP membership lock allows unauthorized member additions in GitLab EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, when the instance-wide SAML or LDAP membership lock was enabled, an authenticated user could have granted or accepted project and group membership outside the identity provider’s control, due to incomplete enforcement of the membership lock on requests created before the lock was enabled.

Impacted Versions: GitLab EE: all versions from 12.0 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 5.9 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N)

Thanks 3nvz for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, an unauthenticated user could have retrieved sensitive internal server credentials due to improper filtering of internal response headers.

Impacted Versions: GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 17.6.5 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 4.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N)

Thanks altair00 for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

CVE-2026-13319 - Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key issue in group milestones API impacts GitLab CE/EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that could have allowed an authenticated user to read milestone metadata, including titles, descriptions, and full project paths, from arbitrary private projects across the instance without any project membership, due to missing authorization checks on a user-supplied project filter parameter in the group milestones API.

Impacted Versions: GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 15.10 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 4.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N)

Thanks a0xnirudh for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

GitLab has remediated an issue that under certain conditions could have allowed an authenticated user to access paid AI features without a valid subscription due to insufficient server-side validation in billing eligibility checks.

Impacted Versions: GitLab EE: all versions from 17.8 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 4.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N)

This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Halil Coban

CVE-2026-105711 - Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information issue in merge request title rendering impacts GitLab CE/EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, when a merge request in a public project referenced a confidential issue from a private project, an authenticated user with no project membership could have read the confidential issue’s title, due to a viewer-independent fragment cache key that incorrectly shared per-user-redacted rendered content across all users.

Impacted Versions: GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 15.0 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 3.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N)

Thanks 20kilograma for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

CVE-2026-14288 - Improper Access Control issue in merge request approval policy enforcement impacts GitLab EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that under certain conditions could have allowed an authenticated user to bypass a required merge request approval policy on a protected branch due to improper access control during approval rule synchronization.

Impacted Versions: GitLab EE: all versions from 17.4 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 3.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N)

Thanks 3nvz for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

CVE-2026-112326 - Improper Cleanup on Thrown Exception issue in security findings impacts GitLab EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with read-only permissions to permanently delete existing vulnerability records due to improper cleanup logic that failed to distinguish between pre-existing records from newly created ones during error handling.

Impacted Versions: GitLab EE: all versions from 17.8 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 3.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N)

This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Gregory Havenga

CVE-2026-103515 - Improper Access Control issue in group Duo admin-lock enforcement for Amazon Q settings impacts GitLab EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, when an instance administrator locked a group’s Duo availability, an authenticated user with group Owner permissions could have re-enabled AI-backed data egress to a third-party service for that group and its descendant projects, due to insufficient granularity of the admin-lock enforcement controls.

Impacted Versions: GitLab EE: all versions from 19.2 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1
CVSS 2.7 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N)

Thanks 3nvz for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

Bug fixes

19.4.3

19.3.6

19.2.9

19.1.9

19.0.10

18.11.13

Important notes on upgrading

This patch includes database migrations that may impact your upgrade process.

Impact on your installation:

Single-node instances: This patch will cause downtime during the upgrade as migrations must complete before GitLab can start.

Multi-node instances: With proper zero-downtime upgrade procedures, this patch can be applied without downtime.

Regular migrations

The following versions include regular migrations that run during the upgrade process:

Post-deploy migrations

The following versions include post-deploy migrations that can run after the upgrade:

To learn more about the impact of upgrades on your installation, see:

Updating

To update GitLab, see the Update page.
To update GitLab Runner, see the Updating the Runner page.

Receive Patch Notifications

To receive patch blog notifications delivered to your inbox, visit our contact us page.
To receive release notifications via RSS, subscribe to our patch release RSS feed or our RSS feed for all releases.

items.text:
Rust Style Guide

This document is a style guide for the usage of the Rust programming language
at Google. In this context, “style” refers to more than just formatting; it
includes guidance on API and implementation design.

Rust is used in many places, including
google3,
Android, ChromeOS, Fuchsia, and Chrome, and we’d like for Rust usage at Google
to be consistent both within and across codebases. In addition to bringing
consistency to our Rust code, style guidance also helps establish a standard of
quality.

Background

Scope

The current scope of authority of the rules outlined in this guide:

In Android, Chromium, and other codebases: This style guide has been
developed in consultation with other codebases, and they intend to start
applying it. These codebases may have their own rules about how strictly
this is expected to be applied. Expect more information here as these
codebases adopt this guide.

Goals of the style guide

By and large, we have this document for
the same reasons we have a C++ style guide.

Most style rules come from one or more of the goals listed below.

Style rules should prioritize readability and maintainability over writeability

We expect our code to be around for long periods of time, and we
consider a little bit of extra effort applied during code writing to be
worth it in the long run if the style rule improves readability.

Style rules should favor better automation

Large-Scale Changes (LSCs)
are common at Google, and consistency helps
make LSCs easier to carry out.

Style rules should be consistent with the wider Rust ecosystem where possible

The broader Rust ecosystem already has a pretty good amount of consistency
in style, and we should rely on that where possible to reduce surprise and make
it less work to learn Google’s Rust style.

Style rules should pull their weight

Every Rust developer and reviewer at Google has to keep these style rules
in mind: as such, we should be careful to include rules that have a tangible
benefit.

Style rules may help avoid minor style disagreements

There are many cases where reasonable people may disagree about a style, and
we expect that disagreement to show up often on CLs. Having a style rule helps
avoid having to rehash this each time. Rules in this category that do not have other
benefits should be kept to a minimum.

Follow public Rust style rules

Follow the official public Rust style rules to the extent they don’t conflict
with this style guide.

A “conflict” would be a case where this style guide suggests a pattern that is
discouraged, or counter to the primary encouraged pattern in the Rust style
guide.

Why does the guidance in this style guide deviate from regular Rust style rules?

Most style guides have three goals: consistency, readability, and encouraging
good API design. Regardless of the specific choices made, it helps everyone to
have these choices made beforehand to limit bikeshedding.

This style guide shares those goals, but it also has an additional goal not seen
as often: smoothing the way for Large-Scale Changes (LSCs). Large codebases like
many of the ones at Google occasionally need to run codebase-spanning
refactorings that are assisted by tooling: for this to work well, the code
should be something tooling has an easy time working with. Consistency helps for
this, but so does having deliberate refactor-friendly patterns.

Apply API design rules in context

When applying rules that relate to API design, you should distinguish two types
of code:

Library code

Intended for use by other projects (applications or other libraries).

Solves a relatively general problem.

Application code

Intended for use in a single application.

Solves a more specific problem.

For library code, style guide rules that concern API design are binding.

For application code, the rules on API design are a strong recommendation. As
you apply them, keep in mind that since application code is written to solve a
specific problem, it should generally favor simplicity and directness over broad
reusability. Avoid premature generalization and abstraction; focus on what is
required to meet the immediate need.

Code organization

Terminology:

A crate is a unit of compilation. A crate always contains a nameless Rust
module, the “root module”.

A Rust module is a unit of code organization within a crate. Rust modules
are used to control visibility of names. Modules can be nested. They can
also be used to split code across files and directories.

The following sections convey that in Chromium, it is preferable to not make
use of all possibilities of splitting modules across files.

Prefer small crates [chrome]

Prefer small crates in Chromium; ideally, but not necessarily, a single file
(focusing on one abstraction). If your code can be split up into small crates,
do so.

A crate corresponds to a single rust_static_library (chrome) rule, which may
contain one or more .rs files.

Additional considerations:

The root module is allowed to re-export public APIs from leaf
submodules, making submodules an implementation detail of the crate (as
users don’t need to know about these submodules).

This rule about small crates applies equally to crates with and without
submodules. First, evaluate whether the APIs need to be in the same crate,
and only then consider whether submodules could help organize the APIs.

If you decide to use submodules, follow the
expected file structure.

Larger crates are allowed when
trait impl coherence rules
force multiple types and traits to be included in one library, or if you’re
building a large foundational library.

Rationale

Fine-grained library targets are recommended in Chromium due to the massive size
of our codebase, non-local effects of adding dependencies in the build graph,
and to improve performance of parallel compilation and build caching.

Use flat file layout for rust_library sources [chrome]

In Chromium .rs source files belonging to one rust_library (one Rust crate)
must reside in a single directory.

Don’t use subdirectories to organize files that belong to a single crate. If
organizing one crate’s files into subdirectories feels necessary, this is a
strong indication that the crate has grown too large and should
be split.

This crate layout is intentionally different from the conventional Cargo
directory structure typically used in open-source repositories.

Exception: Rust code in //third_party that is also built with
Cargo should follow the conventional Cargo
directory structure.

Rationale

The approach in Chromium is driven by the following factors:

Based on the preference for small crates, most
rust_library targets will only contain one source file.

Because of the above point, creating a directory for each rust_library
target would result in most directories containing only one source file.

Multi-file rust_library targets should not create dedicated directories
for submodules either; this ensures a consistent approach.

Name source files and leaf modules after the primary user-defined item

When a leaf module has a primary user-defined item (e.g., Foo), the module
should be named after that item (e.g., mod foo and foo.rs).

Leaf modules that are not primarily about any particular abstraction can be
named as desired.

Rationale

This makes it easy to identify the content/purpose of a source file or leaf
module at a glance.

Don’t implement APIs in non-leaf modules

The only items in non-leaf modules should be module declarations (not
definitions) and re-exports.

Note that the definition of leaf modules allows the following sub-modules:
mod test and cross-language binding modules like #[cxx::bridge].

Exceptions:

Having a small amount of core “ties things together” implementation code in
a non-leaf module may be fine. The goal is to not have a lot of code in
these modules.

Rationale

This makes it easier to find things, and avoids mixing structure and contents.

Don’t use glob imports

Don’t use glob imports, except in the following situations where you may
optionally do so at your own discretion:

use super::* for inline modules

use enum::* in method bodies of enums, and functions that are primarily
dealing with that enum

pub use submodule::* for non-leaf modules

C++ interop: Since the same namespace (in C++) is a submodule in different
Rust crates (in Rust), you may merge the namespaces into a private copy
using glob imports. For example:

mod absl {
pub use status::absl::*;
pub use strings::absl::*;
}

In this hypothetical example, you can use absl::Status and absl::StrCat
from Rust, the same way you would from C++, instead of spelling them as
status::absl::Status and strings::absl::StrCat.

This must only be used for merging C++ namespaces, and the resulting merged
module must not be public.

If using third-party crates that encourage a prelude, it is up to the reviewer’s
discretion to allow it.

This also means that defining preludes should be avoided.

Rationale

Glob imports increase toil for code janitors running LSCs, and make it harder to
know where a type comes from in contexts without xrefs.

A use statement should import items from one module

This rule corresponds to the rustfmt setting imports_granularity = Module.

Basically, there should not be any ::’s inside the {..} block of a use
statement. For example:

use foo::Foo;
use foo::bar::Bar;
use foo::bar::Baz;

use foo::Foo;
use foo::bar::{Bar, Baz};

use foo::{Foo, bar::Bar};

Prefer locally-scoped trait imports

Import traits within function bodies, unless the trait’s methods are used
extensively throughout the file.

fn foo(x: u8) {
// Import the trait within a function, not at the module scope.
use std::str::FromStr;
let string: String = x.parse();
}

Qualify calls to top-level functions with a module name

To use top-level functions defined in other modules or crates, import their
module and call them with modulename::functionname(). For example:

use std::mem;
let x = mem::transmute(y);

use std::mem::transmute;
let x = transmute(y);

Exceptions:

Rationale

Many Rust codebases consistently keep a style such that unqualified lowercase
names are assumed local, so foo() can be assumed to be from the same module.
This rule largely exists to avoid reviewer disagreements, the benefit is mostly
consistency and a minor edge on reading code without xrefs.

Type names should be imported and used unqualified

By default, types and traits should be referenced in code without using their
module path, e.g., code should use Regex, not regex::Regex, with a use
regex::Regex at the top of the file or potentially in the relevant function.

Exceptions:

In cases where there are ambiguities, it is acceptable to directly reference
types with common names like io::Error. It is also acceptable to rename
(use std::io::Error as IoError).

In cases where you have a large “group” of types, e.g. the
hir module in rustc
which contains a large number of HIR types.

In macros and generated code; where requiring a use is counterproductive.

In code with lots of dependencies, where importing everything would lead to
a very large import block with little benefit.

Rationale

This rule largely exists to avoid reviewer disagreements.

Use the appropriate import mechanism [chrome]

Chrome Use chromium::import!().

Code formatting and aesthetics

Use the appropriate formatting tool (e.g., git cl format in Chromium).

Configuration (for style guide authors)

A codebase may choose to not apply the following rustfmt options if they care
about building on stable and the option is unavailable on their stable Rust:

Maximum of 100 columns per line:
max_width = 100

Usage of lowercase alphabets in hex literals (0xab123cdef as opposed to
0xAB123CDEF):
hex_literal_case = Lower

Macro matcher formatting:
format_macro_matchers = true

Usage of escapes for invisible characters in literals. E.g., if you wish to
have text containing a Zero-Width joiner, use \u{200D}.

Opting out of automatic formatting

You may opt out of automatic formatting using #[rustfmt::skip], but only in
the following situations:

Manual alignment – If you have a situation-specific reason to have a
snippet of code line up in a particular way (e.g., multiple similar lines of
code that you want to remain aligned for readability, or a
matrix-constructing function).

Generated code (ideally, use a genrule instead).

Important: Formatting should not be skipped for personal style choices.

Ownership and borrowing

Avoid Rc and Arc

Prefer unique ownership and borrowing over Rc and Arc for managing memory.

Exception:

Use Rc and Arc when the alternative ownership and borrowing structure
would be unreasonably complex to write, understand, or maintain. This is a
judgment call to be discussed during code review.

Rationale

Generally, Rust allows representing object graphs without using shared ownership
smart pointers. These pointers add runtime overhead and their own unique
complexity. Engineers coming from other languages might tend to use Rc and
Arc too quickly.

Prefer borrows over deep copies

Use .clone() when you genuinely need a deep copy of an object.

Avoid using .clone() as a substitute for borrowing. Design code that works
naturally with Rust’s ownership and borrowing rules. However, if the borrowing
relationships become excessively complex, .clone() can be a pragmatic choice.

Consider the performance needs of the code while choosing between cloning and
borrowing.

Note: This advice does not apply to cloning Rc or Arc pointers. Cloning
reference-counted pointers does not create a deep copy, and is an expected way
to use them.

Rationale

Deep copies can be expensive to make due to memory allocation and data copying.

Function inputs and outputs

Accept flexible references for immutable data

When functions accept borrowed, immutable data, use a reference type that
affords the most flexibility. Pass references to the data itself instead of
references to smart pointers, containers, or wrappers.

Use

Instead of

Why?

&T

&Box<T>

Borrow the data inside the box

&[T]

&Vec<T>

Accept any slice instead of specific containers

&str

&String

Accept a string slice instead of references to owned strings

Option<&T>

&Option<T>

Borrow the data inside the Option

Exceptions:

When expecting non-linear character data such as Rope/Cord.

For context, see Clippy lints
borrowed_box
and
ptr_arg.

Rationale

Accepting reference types that don’t mention specific smart pointers,
containers, or wrappers makes functions more versatile and performant: callers
can pass data held in a variety of ways without copying it first.

Iterators vs. owned collections in return types

Prefer returning iterators (either concrete types or impl Iterator) where
possible over returning Vec<T>.

Note: In application code, returning a Vec<T> is fine if it simplifies the
code and if flexibility and performance advantages of iterators are not clearly
needed.

Exceptions:

Most callers will need to construct an owned vector.

The function’s implementation naturally constructs a vector.

The returned value will likely need to be randomly indexed.

The algorithm works better as a for loop and the forced allocation doesn’t
matter too much.

The function’s intended purpose is creating a new owned collection.

The function is returning a pre-existing vector.

Rationale

Highly reusable library code generally should strive to provide more flexible
and performant APIs. Returning an iterator allows callers to choose how to
consume the data: collect it into a vector, process it in a loop, or chain
further iterator adapters. Some of these options allow users to avoid
unnecessary allocations.

In application code, the usage patterns for a function are often easier to
predict. If it is clear that performance is not a concern, or that data would be
collected into a vector anyway, returning a vector makes for a simpler API.

Iterators vs. slices in function parameters

Highly reusable library code should accept iterators or impl IntoIterator if
it only needs to iterate over the input.

Note: In application code, accepting a slice &[T] is fine if it simplifies the
code and if flexibility and performance advantages of iterators are not clearly
needed.

Rationale

Highly reusable library code generally should strive to provide more flexible
and performant APIs. Functions that accept iterators offer callers:

More flexibility (data can be supplied from any collection)

Efficiency (data does not need to be copied into a contiguous piece of
memory)

Composability (the function works better with iterator chains)

In application code, the usage patterns for a function are often easier to
predict. If it is clear that performance is not a concern, or that callers would
always have a vector anyway, accepting a slice makes for a simpler API.

Accepting Into

When designing library APIs that accept a T but users are likely to have
various types, consider accepting impl Into<T> instead of T if call-site
ergonomics are paramount.

Tip: This should be balanced against code bloat concerns; it is not a
requirement to use lots of Into<T> in your code.

Note: Application code should almost never use impl Into<T> parameters.

Rationale

Using impl Into<T> allows a function to directly accept various arguments of
various compatible types. For example, a function accepting impl Into<String>
could be called with a String or a &str literal directly.

The tradeoff here is balancing the convenience of avoiding a .into() at the
callsite against the cost of generics (more complex API signature, increased
code size, sometimes even type inference difficulties).

Prefer enum over bool in APIs

Use enum function parameters instead of bool in cases where the purpose of
the parameter is not obvious.

If you do use bool, consider using an inline comment to document the purpose
of the bool in an argument list.

Reporting errors

Choose the error reporting mechanism that fits your API contract: Option,
Result, or panic!.

Use Option for simple failures where the cause is obvious and the caller
would not benefit from further details. This is best for standard, anticipated
outcomes like a missing value or a parsing mismatch.

// Good: The cause of the failure is obvious (integer overflow). No further
// details could be reasonably provided.
fn checked_add(a: u32, b: u32) -> Option<u32> { ... }

Use Result for recoverable failures where the caller needs context to
handle the error. These are often “unavoidable” errors caused by external
factors (like I/O or network) that even correctly implemented code cannot
prevent with checks ahead of time. Nevertheless, the caller can reasonably
anticipate the kinds of errors (a file-related function can fail with an I/O
error). The error details allow the caller to distinguish failure modes and
recover appropriately.

// Good: The caller needs to know *why* it failed (NotFound vs PermissionDenied).
fn open_file(path: &Path) -> Result<File, io::Error> { ... }

Use panic! to report bugs and violated invariants. These errors are
avoidable: the program is missing a check, and is calling an operation without
fulfilling a precondition. These defects must be fixed in the code, not handled
at runtime, although coarse-grained recovery might be possible with
catch_unwind.

// Good: Panics if the invariant (index must be in bounds) is violated.
// This indicates a bug in the caller's logic.
impl<T> MyVec<T> {
pub fn remove(&mut self, index: usize) -> T {
if index >= self.len() {
panic!("index out of bounds");
}
// ...
}
}

Note: Some codebases may choose to avoid panics entirely, and require even
broken invariants to be reported via Result.

Exceptions:

Developer-facing binaries may use panics for non-fatal errors.

Tests may use panics for assertions.

Types

Newtypes versus type aliases

Use a
newtype
instead of a type alias in the following cases:

If the type you are defining has notable semantic differences.

For types that warrant an API of their own.

If you want the flexibility to change the underlying type later, especially
if you don’t control all usages of your type.

For type safety, if it’s easy for the types to get mixed up. For example, a
Date type may use newtypes to distinguish Day, Month, and Year
numbers in its internal calculations.

Prefer named fields over tuples and non-newtype tuple structs

Prefer types with named fields over tuples, as tuple indexes (.0, .1, …)
quickly become confusing.

Exceptions:

Newtype tuple structs (tuple structs with only one field).

In very local contexts where there is unlikely to be any confusion.

Traits

Add trait implementations when they become necessary

As a general rule, low-level library code should anticipate users’ needs
proactively, while application code should add trait impls as needed.

Implement known standard library traits instead of custom methods

If a method matches the purpose and behavior of a standard library trait,
implement that trait. For example, instead of writing fn from_str(&str) ->
Self on Foo, you should impl FromStr for Foo.

It is acceptable to have both the method and the trait impl for discoverability
reasons.

For context, see Clippy lint
should_implement_trait
(list of traits).

Use #[derive()] if possible

Manual implementations should be avoided if they can be expressed as a
#[derive()].

Generics versus dyn Trait

In libraries, prefer accepting generics (T: Trait or impl Trait) in function
parameters over dyn Trait.

Exceptions:

Cases where code size matters.

Rationale

Efficiency

Additional indirection: Creating a dyn Trait requires setting up a fat
pointer, and a vtable lookup is required for every call of a function on
the trait.

If a function takes a dyn Trait, the compiler can’t perform certain
optimizations that it could if the function was generic, such as
inlining calls to functions of the trait.

Some traits are not
dyn compatible.
For example, a trait is not dyn compatible if it has generic functions,
associated functions without a self parameter, or functions that return
Self.

When to define a trait versus an inherent implementation

Define a trait only for the following purposes:

To enable generic programming (to use T: Trait in constraints of generic
functions and types).

To accept or return an impl Trait or dyn Trait.

To define an extension trait (but see also the caveats
in the section on extension traits).

In all other cases where you want to implement functionality for a type, use an
inherent implementation.

Don’t use traits merely to organize code.

Extension traits

An
extension trait
is a trait that adds methods to a type from a different crate.

What differentiates an extension trait from other traits is that its sole
purpose is to add methods to the type; it is not intended for use in generics
(T: Trait, impl Trait) or dynamic dispatch (dyn Trait). To indicate this,
the name of an extension trait should carry the suffix ~Ext (for example,
ForeignTypeExt).

In general, the team that owns the original type should also own the extension
trait.

Exceptions:

Extension methods that are expected to become well known and provide
significant value, for example, in foundational libraries / frameworks.

Note: This rule is specifically about extension traits. It is relatively common
to define a trait as an input trait (e.g., DateLike) and implement it on a
bunch of foreign types.

Examples

extern crate foreign_crate;
use foreign_crate::ForeignType;
trait ForeignTypeExt {
fn additional_method(&self);
}
impl ForeignTypeExt for ForeignType {
fn additional_method(&self) { ... }
}

It is also possible to define an extension trait for every type that implements
some foreign trait. Effectively, this is equivalent to adding default methods to
the foreign trait:

extern crate foreign_crate;
use foreign_crate::ForeignTrait;
trait ForeignTraitExt {
fn additional_method(&self);
}
impl<T: ForeignTrait> ForeignTraitExt for T {
fn additional_method(&self) { ... }
}

Rationale

When the same team owns the extension trait and the type being extended, this
helps avoid method name conflicts between the base type and the extension trait
or between two extension traits.

Specific guidance for important traits

Types with public fields: Consider implementing traits implemented by
all subfields.

Error types: Implement the Copy trait whenever possible. Copy types
are simpler to manage and propagate because they can be passed by value
without moving ownership. An example of a case where this is not possible is
if the error must contain non-Copy fields like a String.

Copy: Implement whenever it is reasonably clear that the type will
continue to be Copy in the future.

Clone: Most types should implement Clone unless they represent some
external resource.

Default: Implement if the type implements new() or otherwise has a
default state. For context, see Clippy lint
new_without_default.

PartialEq / Eq: If you want users to use the == operator,
prefer implementing PartialEq over Eq. When you do implement Eq, be
aware of the additionally required reflexivity (details:
https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Eq.html).

PartialOrd / Ord: If you want users to use the < or >
operators, prefer implementing PartialOrd over Ord. When you do
implement Ord, be aware that it requires total ordering (details:
https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Ord.html).

Map keys

If you think it is likely that a type will be used as a map key or
otherwise cached, implement Hash and Eq.

If, in addition, the type has a clear total ordering, implement Ord
(and any traits it needs).

Pair important From impls with explicit constructor methods

If a type has an important From impl that is expected to be one of the primary
ways of constructing it, add an inherent ::new(), ::new_from_foo()¸ or
::from_foo() method.

Options structs should implement Default

Structs with all-public fields that are primarily used as a “bag of options” for
a function should implement Default.

Rationale

This enables convenient use of struct update syntax (Struct { a: 0,
..Default::default()} ).

Concurrency

Handling poison

Never reach inside a poisoned mutex to get at its insides, no matter how
tempting the use case may seem.

Don’t use async / .await [chrome]

Don’t use async / .await in Chromium.

Don’t start new threads through the Rust standard library [chrome]

In Chromium, prefer to use sequences instead of threads.

Use fuchsia_sync::Mutex [Fuchsia]

Use Fuchsia’s mutex type, rather than one from std::sync or parking_lot.

Macros

When considering how to express an API, prefer in order:

Regular Rust functions, types, traits, objects, and modules. (Avoid macros,
code generation, and metaprogramming where possible).

macro_rules!-style macros.

Other code generation strategies (e.g. genrule)

proc_macro macros.

When you decide to use a macro or code generation, please weigh the benefits
against the costs:

IDEs, Code Search and other developer tools will work less well on code that
uses macros.

Macros can create dialects of the language that make it harder for engineers
to work across the codebase.

Large scale changes are more difficult and expensive to apply.

Rationale

Prefer non-macro facilities: Macros can create dialects of the language that
make it harder for engineers to work across the codebase. When a reader sees a
usage of a macro, they can make fewer assumptions about that code than if it
didn’t use a macro. Macros are harder to write correctly than regular Rust code.

Use macro_rules! for simple code generation: Since Rust macros operate on
the AST, they can be less fragile than textual code generation.

Naming

Naming methods

Follow the Rust standard library style for naming methods. See also the guidance
on
naming conventions
in the Comprehensive Rust course.

Specific considerations:

Use prefixes such as as_...(), to_...(), or into_...() with the
appropriate self convention. See also
this section
of the Rust API Guidelines and the Clippy lint
wrong_self_convention.

Naming lifetimes

Lifetimes should have descriptive names, especially type lifetimes.

Exceptions:

Type lifetimes that are extremely generic abstractions like Cow.

It is fine to use anonymous lifetimes ('_) where they work.

Single-character lifetimes are okay when they are simply expressing the
relationship between a method’s input and output, or needed for a local
higher-ranked lifetime bounds (for<'a>). Up to two such local lifetimes
are fine, if more are needed, we strongly advise you to use descriptive
names.

Naming generic parameters

Use a short name for your generic parameters (either single or multi character),
related to the kind of thing they represent. Single-letter generics are okay,
but the letter chosen should be somewhat indicative of the object type, ideally
taken from the most important trait bound.

T or U are fine when the generics are in a relatively unbound context; i.e.
it is an API intended for use with most types, like Vec<T>.

Naming extension traits

When naming an extension trait, give the name an ~Ext
suffix (for example, ForeignTypeExt).

Naming initialization functions

Follow these guidelines when naming initialization functions:

Constructors: Use new(), or new_with_foo() if there is more than one. If
the constructor returns a Result, use try_new().

Value-to-value conversions: Use from_foo() with an associated From impl.
See
here
for details on when an operation can be considered to be a value-to-value
conversion.

Avoid abbreviations

Don’t use abbreviations (especially acronyms and initialisms) that someone
outside your project is unlikely to know. Don’t abbreviate by deleting letters
within a word.

See also the
Google C++ Style Guide.

Exceptions:

Common abbreviations found in Wikipedia.

Abbreviations that are unlikely to be confusing to people outside of your
project, for example IpAddr. You and your reviewer should make this
