items.text:
The official CLI for the OpenAI REST API.

brew install openai/tools/openai

To test or install the CLI locally, you need Go version 1.26 or later installed.

go install 'github.com/openai/openai-cli/cmd/openai@latest'

Once you have run go install, the binary is placed in your Go bin directory:

Default location: $HOME/go/bin (or $GOPATH/bin if GOPATH is set)

Check your path: Run go env GOPATH to see the base directory

If commands aren't found after installation, add the Go bin directory to your PATH:

# Add to your shell profile (.zshrc, .bashrc, etc.)
export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"

The first eligible interactive openai run quietly saves image picker Tab
shortcuts for future Bash, zsh, and fish sessions. Open a new terminal to use
them. See shortcut setup and removal for
requirements and opt-out. PowerShell keeps normal Tab completion; press Enter
after openai images generate to open the picker.

Bare openai checks for newer stable releases when stdin, stdout, and stderr are terminals.
It adds a plain-text notice below help, at most once every seven days.
Explicit help, commands, completion, CI, and redirected streams skip the check entirely.

The notice includes an update command when the CLI can verify its installation method.
Verified Homebrew installations use brew upgrade --cask openai/tools/openai.
Go commands require a verified binary, an available Go command, and an explicit matching GOBIN.
Custom GOOS or GOARCH settings select the installation guide instead.
Go upgrades to major version 2 or later also select the installation guide.
Unknown installations receive the installation-guide link instead.
The CLI never installs updates automatically.

Checks use public GitHub release metadata without API credentials, at most once daily.
Checks respect HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY, including their lowercase forms.
Update discovery waits at most 200 milliseconds. Failed checks remain silent.
Package-manager availability can lag a new GitHub release.
Set OPENAI_CLI_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to disable checks and notices.

After cloning the git repository for this project, you can use the
scripts/run script to run the tool locally:

The CLI follows a resource-based command structure:

openai <resource> [subresource...] <command> [flags...]

Standard API endpoints require an API key:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
openai responses create \
--input "Say this is a test" \
--model gpt-5.5

Admin endpoints require an admin API key:

export OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY="sk-admin-..."
openai admin organization usage completions \
--start-time 1735689600 \
--end-time 1735776000 \
--bucket-width 1d

Browse each group with --help, for example openai admin --help or
openai admin organization --help. Existing colon commands such as
openai admin:organization:usage completions continue to work.

Run openai to browse command groups by task, with descriptions for each group.
Group help separates actions from nested command groups and lists every immediate command.
Help works without an API key or network connection:

openai help setup # Enter your API key safely
openai images generate --help # Example and every image option
openai help images generate # The same complete image help
openai --help # Command groups and global options

Add --help (or -h) to any command for its complete help page.
openai help COMMAND shows the same page.
Command pages list global options. Use openai --help for their full descriptions.
You can place --help after valid command options.
The old help --all spelling prints migration guidance and the complete page.
Command behavior, defaults, and output formats remain unchanged.
Tab completion follows the same group order and supports help topics and file input paths.
After upgrading, reload shell completion to enable the new file-path behavior.
Older loaded completion scripts keep their previous behavior until refreshed.

Enable command insertion to fill your command line
from examples, setup guidance, and recovery commands. Ctrl+X, then Tab searches suggestions
without running them. Double Tab is an optional binding for Bash, zsh, and fish.

Successful JSON responses print readable text by default, including in pipes.
Use --format json or --format jsonl in scripts that parse API data.
See reading command results for extraction, binary
output, and the scope of readable presentation.

Upload a local file with an explicit purpose, inspect its metadata, then download its contents:

openai files upload "upload space.txt" --purpose user_data
openai files get file-example
openai files download file-example --output "downloaded copy.txt"
openai files download file-example > copy.txt

Replace file-example with the returned file ID. Upload takes a plain path, without an added @.
create, retrieve, content, and their existing flags remain available.
See working with files for literal filenames, output formats, and script examples.

openai images generate --prompt "A tiny orange robot" saves images to
~/Downloads/gpt-images/ and prints their paths, including in pipes. The CLI
uses gpt-image-2.5-sunburst when saving without an explicit model or legacy
response format. Use --model for another exact ID, --name for a filename,
or --output-dir for an existing directory. Existing files are kept.
--format json returns API data without saving or applying the CLI preset.
images edit also saves new results while keeping source files.
images create-variation is retired and no longer available. To create a
variation, use images edit with a GPT Image model and a prompt. See
image generation and saving for commands
and defaults.

openai images preview "path/to/image.png" redisplays a saved image without an
API request. Use openai images inline on or off to remember whether future
saved images appear automatically. Per-command --inline auto, on or off
overrides that setting. on also permits an image font in local Apple Terminal.

Errors print actionable summaries to stderr by default. Use --format-error json
for original API error details, including unknown fields and SDK-reported stream
error events. For those events, extraction paths include the error envelope,
for example --transform-error error.code. Explicit --format
values json, jsonl, raw, and yaml also apply to errors unless overridden
by --format-error; an explicit --format-error auto or text restores summaries.
--transform-error extracts error data independently of successful output.
Malformed or empty error bodies receive a safe diagnostic; HTTP status is included
only when the SDK retains it. Summaries omit rejected values and request URLs;
explicit API error details can contain server-supplied sensitive data.

Environment variable

Required

Default value

OPENAI_API_KEY

no

null

OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY

no

null

OPENAI_ORG_ID

no

null

OPENAI_PROJECT_ID

no

null

OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET

no

null

OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS

no

null

OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_FILE

no

null

OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_FILE

no

null

OPENAI_UNTRUSTED_STDIN

no

false

--api-key (can also be set with OPENAI_API_KEY env var)

--admin-api-key (can also be set with OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY env var)

--organization (can also be set with OPENAI_ORG_ID env var)

--project (can also be set with OPENAI_PROJECT_ID env var)

--webhook-secret (can also be set with OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET env var)

--mtls-client-cert-file (can also be set with OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_FILE env var)

--mtls-client-key-file (can also be set with OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_FILE env var)

--help - Show command line usage

--debug - Enable debug logging. This includes HTTP request/response details and bodies; do not share debug logs if they may contain sensitive payloads.

--version, -v - Show the CLI version

--base-url - Use a custom API backend URL. HTTPS is required except for
localhost or literal loopback IP addresses such as 127.0.0.1 and ::1.
This also applies to OPENAI_BASE_URL; remote HTTP backends must enable HTTPS.

--header, -H - Add a literal request header as Name: Value; repeat for multiple headers

--format - Change the output format (auto, text, explore, json, jsonl, pretty, raw, yaml); auto selects readable text unless extracting data

--format-error - Change the stderr error format (auto, text, explore, json, jsonl, pretty, raw, yaml); auto selects readable summaries unless extracting error data

--transform - Transform the data output using GJSON syntax

--transform-error - Transform the error output using GJSON syntax

Use --header or -H before or after a resource command:

openai --header 'X-Trace-ID: example-123' models list \
-H 'X-Client-Label: local,manual'

Values are literal: commas and colons are preserved, and @ prefixes do not
read files. Surrounding spaces and tabs are trimmed from values. -H 'X-Example:'
sends an empty value. If a name is repeated, the last value wins regardless of
case, overriding default and endpoint-specific headers. Headers managed by the
HTTP transport, such as Host and Content-Length, retain the transport's
behavior. Supplied header values are hidden in help and redacted in debug logs.

For credential-bearing headers, have a secret manager or trusted launcher set
OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS directly in the CLI's environment. This keeps credentials
out of command arguments and avoids typing literal secrets into shell history.
The variable accepts one Name: Value entry per line. For example, with
non-sensitive values:

export OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS='X-Trace-ID: example-123
X-Client-Label: local,manual'
openai models list

--header and endpoint-specific header flags override matching environment
entries. Environment header values are also redacted in debug logs. Use
OPENAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY for standard API and admin authentication.

Mutual TLS is currently in beta. To opt in and activate a CA certificate for
your organization or project, follow the
OpenAI Mutual TLS Beta Program
instructions.

To authenticate API-key requests with a mutual TLS client certificate, provide
the client certificate and private key as separate PEM files. If certificate
chain support is enabled for your organization, the certificate file must
contain the leaf certificate first, followed by any intermediate certificates.
Otherwise, use a client certificate signed directly by an activated CA
certificate.

export OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_FILE=/run/secrets/openai/client-chain.pem
export OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/openai/client.key
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://mtls.api.openai.com/v1
openai files list

Both mTLS files must be configured together. Keep the private key in a
permission-restricted file; do not put private-key contents directly in command
arguments or environment variables. The CLI does not automatically select an
mTLS endpoint, so configure OPENAI_BASE_URL or --base-url explicitly. HTTP
and SOCKS proxies remain supported, but HTTPS proxies are rejected to prevent
presenting the client certificate during the proxy's own TLS handshake.

Passing files as arguments

For JSON input values, @myfile.ext reads local file contents:

Binary upload flags use plain paths. For example, use files upload --file "upload space.txt" --purpose user_data.
Here, --file "@upload space.txt" names an actual file starting with @; it does not expand another file reference.
See working with files.

openai <command> --arg @abe.jpg

Files can also be passed inside JSON or YAML blobs:

openai <command> --arg '{image: "@abe.jpg"}'
# Equivalent:
openai <command> <<YAML
arg:
image: "@abe.jpg"
YAML

When piping JSON or YAML from an untrusted source, enable untrusted-stdin mode:

untrusted-producer | OPENAI_UNTRUSTED_STDIN=1 openai <command> --file ./upload.txt

In this mode, values supplied through stdin are treated as literal data: @,
@file://, and @data:// references in request bodies, headers, and query
parameters do not read local files. File-upload parameters must be provided
explicitly as command-line flags. Explicit flags retain their normal file
behavior and take precedence over values supplied through stdin. Leave
OPENAI_UNTRUSTED_STDIN unset when using trusted heredocs or other trusted
piped input that intentionally references local files.

If you need to pass a string literal that begins with an @ sign, you can
escape the @ sign to avoid accidentally passing a file.

openai <command> --username '\@abe'

For JSON endpoints, the CLI tool does filetype sniffing to determine whether the
file contents should be sent as a string literal (for plain text files) or as a
base64-encoded string literal (for binary files). If you need to explicitly send
the file as either plain text or base64-encoded data, you can use
@file://myfile.txt (for string encoding) or @data://myfile.dat (for
base64-encoding). Note that absolute paths will begin with @file:// or
@data://, followed by a third / (for example, @file:///tmp/file.txt).

openai <command> --arg @data://file.txt

Linking different Go SDK versions

You can link the CLI against a different version of the OpenAI Go SDK
for development purposes using the ./scripts/link script.

To link to a specific version from a repository (version can be a branch,
git tag, or commit hash):

./scripts/link github.com/org/repo@version

To link to a local copy of the SDK:

./scripts/link ../path/to/openai-go

If you run the link script without any arguments, it will default to ../openai-go.

Please share bug reports and feature requests through GitHub issues.
Pull requests are limited to repository collaborators; we do not accept pull requests from non-collaborators.
See CONTRIBUTING.md for the contribution policy and development guide.
For security vulnerabilities, follow SECURITY.md.

Copyright 2026 OpenAI

This project is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

Passing files as arguments
For JSON input values, @myfile.ext reads local file contents:

items.title: The compiler was supposed to end programming too
items.author: theanonymousone
items.summary:
It’s 7:40 on a Tuesday morning in 2031, and you haven’t written a line of code yet. You probably won’t today, and that’s fine.

While you slept, four agents
items.text:
It’s 7:40 on a Tuesday morning in 2031, and you haven’t written a line of code yet. You probably won’t today, and that’s fine.

While you slept, four agents worked through the backlog you sorted yesterday afternoon. Three of them finished. Their pull requests are waiting for you, each with the tests it added, a short recording of the feature working, and a note about the parts it wasn’t sure of. The fourth agent stopped at 2:13 a.m. and left you a question instead:

The spec says refunds go back to the original card. This customer’s card expired in March. What should happen?

The agent could write refund code all day long. What it can’t do is decide what your company owes a customer whose card has expired, so it stopped and asked, which is exactly what you’d want from a new hire too. Your morning goes like this: you read three pull requests, you go and talk to someone in support, and you write the rule down so clearly that nobody (human or otherwise) has to guess again.

Imagined · Tuesday, 2031

22:0002:0006:0010:0014:0018:0022:00

Agents

122:00 Three agents work through yesterday's backlog and open three pull requests, each with tests and a recording.

222:00 A fourth agent stops and leaves a question: refunds go to the original card, but that card expired.

313:00 Agents build the refund rule you wrote down, with the tests you wrote first.

421:30 Tonight's runs start from the plan you approved.

You

507:40 Read the three pull requests and watch the recordings.

609:00 Answer the 02:13 question. You can't, yet.

710:00 Ask support what customers with expired cards expect.

811:00 Write the rule down as a short spec and five tests.

914:00 Read the agents' work on the one part that touches money.

1016:30 Approve tonight's plan. Go home.

I made that Tuesday up. None of it is science fiction, though. Agents that work unattended overnight exist today, and one of them runs on my own machine every night at ten. It invents a small project, builds it, tests it, and I find out what it made over breakfast. The first morning, I had no idea what it had built. That build is now Rule Safari, a live project on this site, with an article explaining how it works.

So is this the end of programming? People have been asking that for more than seventy years. I find that comforting. I also find it a little suspicious.

Programming has been ending since 1954

On 10 November 1954, IBM’s Programming Research Group finished a preliminary report on a new language called FORTRAN. One sentence in it says that FORTRAN “should virtually eliminate coding and debugging.”

I love this sentence. It’s so sure of itself, and it even came with a budget: problems solved “for less than half the cost” of doing it without FORTRAN. The industry had a name for this kind of thing back then. Assemblers and compilers were called automatic programming. You’d describe what you wanted, and the machine would write the program.

FORTRAN shipped in 1957, and it really did eliminate a kind of coding. Almost nobody translates formulas into machine instructions by hand anymore. Debugging survived just fine. (This month I chased a Scry bug that came down to a bookmark saved only every twelve hours, so I can confirm debugging is alive and well.)

What FORTRAN actually did was take one tedious part of the job away and move the job up a level. People stopped thinking about registers and started thinking about bigger problems. Programs got cheaper to write, so everybody wanted more of them. That has happened over and over since.

Assembly languageYou stopped: writing instructions as raw numbersKathleen Booth, "Coding for A.R.C."

1947

FORTRANYou stopped: translating formulas into machine instructions by handThe 1954 report: it "should virtually eliminate coding and debugging."

1957

CYou stopped: rewriting the same program for every new machine

1972

The Last OneYou stopped: nothing, as it turned outA BASIC program generator, named as the last program you would ever need to buy.

1981

Stack OverflowYou stopped: solving every error message alone

2008

npmYou stopped: writing your own everything

2010

GitHub CopilotYou stopped: typing the boilerplate

2021

Coding agentsYou stopped: typing most of the code

2025

NextYou stopped: ?

20??

My favorite rung is 1981. A British company called D.J. “AI” Systems (yes, really) sold a BASIC program generator named The Last One. The name was the whole pitch. It would write all your programs for you, so it would be the last program you’d ever need to buy.

Reviewers found it useful for some business programs. It was not the last one.

Here’s the pattern on every rung. Something gets automated, the people doing the work stop doing that thing by hand, and the field keeps growing anyway. GitHub counted more than 180 million developers in its 2025 report, and more than 36 million of them had joined in the previous twelve months.

So I don’t think AI ends programming. I do think this rung is different in one way, and that’s speed. GitHub Copilot’s preview came out in June 2021. By 2025, 84% of developers in Stack Overflow’s survey were using AI tools or planning to. Four years, from novelty to default.

What 2026 actually looks like

The vibes are loud right now, so let’s start with numbers. (Speaking of vibes: Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” in February 2025, for the kind of coding where you “fully give in to the vibes.” Stack Overflow asked about it that year. 72% of developers said it isn’t part of their professional work, and another 5% said emphatically no. I love that they offered that option.)

Stack Overflow’s survey is the biggest regular check-up we have, and the adoption curve in it is steep: from 70% of developers using AI tools or planning to in 2023, to 84% in 2025, when half of professional developers were using them every day.

You’d think all that use would mean developers love these tools. Nope. Favorable sentiment fell from 77% in 2023 to 60% in 2025, and only ticked back up to 62% this year. In 2025, more developers distrusted the accuracy of AI output (46%) than trusted it (33%). The top frustration, picked by 66% of them, was “AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite.”

I feel seen. Almost right is an expensive kind of wrong, because you have to read every line to find the part that isn’t. (45% of them said debugging AI-generated code takes longer.)

20%40%60%80%100%202320242025202670%76%84%use or plan to77%72%60%62%favorable42%43%33%trust accuracy

Then there’s my favorite study of the whole AI boom, mostly because it’s so rude. In early 2025, METR, a nonprofit research group, ran a proper randomized controlled trial. Sixteen experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues in their own repositories, projects they’d been on for years, and each issue was randomly assigned to allow AI tools or ban them.

Before they started, the developers expected AI to cut their time by 24%. When they finished, they believed it had cut it by 20%. The clock said that with AI they took 19% longer.

Nineteen percent longer! And they walked away sure it had helped.

← longershorter →

Economists predictedexpert forecast39% less time

ML researchers predictedexpert forecast38% less time

The developers expectedbefore the tasks24% less time

The developers feltafter the tasks20% less time

The clock measuredwhat happened19% more time

Before anyone screenshots that for a hot take: it’s one study of sixteen people, using early-2025 tools, on codebases they knew better than any model could.

And METR tried to run it again. A bigger study started in August 2025, with 57 developers and more than 800 tasks, and in February 2026 METR said the data was too unreliable to lean on. Mostly that was because developers kept declining to take part, since they “do not wish to work without AI.” The early numbers hinted at an 18% speedup for the returning developers (with a range wide enough to include no speedup at all).

I think that’s the most 2026 way an experiment has ever failed. People refused to be in the group without AI.

What I take from METR is narrower than any headline, and more useful: how fast you feel is not a measurement. If you want to know whether AI makes your team faster, measure it the way you’d measure anything else.

The line that keeps going up

METR’s other big project tracks how long a task an AI agent can finish on its own. They time human experts on a suite of software tasks, then find the task length where an agent succeeds half the time. In 2019, GPT-2 managed tasks that take a person about three seconds. GPT-4 got to about four minutes in 2023. Claude 3.7 Sonnet reached an hour in February 2025, and Claude Opus 4.6 reached about twelve hours a year later.

Across the whole series, that number has doubled about every six months. Since 2023, it’s been closer to every four months.

1 min1 hour1 workday1 work week1 work month2019202120232025202720292031if the trend holdsGPT-2GPT-4Claude 3.7 SonnetGPT-5Claude Opus 4.6

Now, a log-scale chart with a dashed line on the end is how a lot of bad predictions start, so let me be careful. “Half the time” is doing a lot of work in that definition. Benchmark tasks are cleaner than your codebase. And METR stopped updating that page in September. But if the line keeps going even roughly, agents will handle a month of human work, half the time, around 2028. That’s where my 2031 Tuesday comes from. I didn’t pull it out of thin air. I pulled it out of a log-scale chart, which is thin air with axes.

The companies building these things are already living a version of it. Google said in October 2024 that more than a quarter of its new code was generated by AI, and “well over 30%” six months later. In March 2025, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei predicted AI would be writing 90% of code within three to six months. That was too soon. But by May 2026, Anthropic said more than 80% of the code merged into its own codebase was written by Claude.

When code gets cheap, the queue moves

Make one step of a process faster and the work piles up in front of the next slowest step. Anyone who has worked a kitchen on a Saturday night knows this: speed up the grill and the plates start waiting at the pass.

That’s what’s happening to software teams. In 2025, Faros AI looked at telemetry from more than 10,000 developers on 1,255 teams. Developers on teams with high AI adoption finished 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests, and their review time went up 91%.

Faros ran it again in 2026 with 22,000 developers. Task completion per developer was up 34%, which sounds great until you read the rest. Median review time had grown five times. 31% more pull requests were merging without any review at all, and the ratio of incidents to pull requests had more than tripled.

The code got cheaper, the reading got more expensive, and some teams quietly stopped reading. That matters because the code isn’t always good. Veracode tested more than 100 language models on 80 coding tasks in 2025, and 45% of the results had a security flaw. GitClear found that copy-pasted lines went from 8.3% of changed code in 2021 to 12.3% in 2024, while moved code, the kind you get from refactoring, fell from about a quarter to under 10%.

Spare a thought for the maintainers, too. Daniel Stenberg, who leads curl, started banning people who submitted “AI slop” bug reports in May 2025, writing that the project was “effectively being DDoSed.” In January 2026, curl shut down its bug bounty.

201920262031, a guess

Decide what to build

Write it down

Write the code

Review it

Check it works

Ship and run it

Today: code arrives faster than people can read it, so pull requests wait for review.

Fred Brooks saw a version of this coming in 1986. In “No Silver Bullet” he split the difficulties of software into two piles, borrowing Aristotle’s words: essence and accidents. The accidents are the trouble our tools cause us, like syntax, boilerplate and fighting the build. The essence is what he called “the specification, design, and testing of this conceptual construct,” which is a fancy way of saying: working out what the thing should do. AI is getting very good at the accidents. The essence is the refund question from 2:13 a.m., and it’s still on your desk.

The rung we might be sawing off

This is the part of the data I like least.

In August 2025, Erik Brynjolfsson and two colleagues at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab used ADP payroll data to look at who was getting hired. Employment for software developers aged 22 to 25 was down nearly 20% from its peak in late 2022. Older developers showed no noticeable change.

They updated the study this August, with data through June 2026. Young workers in AI-exposed jobs are now 19% below where they’d be if they had kept pace with less-exposed peers. Experienced workers show no comparable gap. Most of the effect comes from companies hiring fewer young people in the first place.

The rest of the market isn’t exactly roaring either. Indeed’s index of software development job postings sits about 21% below February 2020, after bottoming out 39% below in May 2025.

The Stanford authors are careful to call their findings descriptive, not causal, and plenty else has happened since 2022. Interest rates went up, and a lot of companies had hired too many people during the pandemic (Indeed’s index peaked at more than twice its 2020 level in early 2022). But the pattern lines up uncomfortably well with what agents are good at: the small, well-defined ticket we used to give the new person on the team.

Senior engineers get made on the job, mostly by being juniors on real teams: doing the boring tickets, breaking production once, and having someone kind explain why. If agents take all the boring tickets, where does the next senior engineer come from? It’s hard to review code well if you’ve never written much of it.

I don’t have a clean answer. My guess is that the teams doing well in 2035 will be the ones that kept hiring juniors in 2026 and gave them a different apprenticeship: reviewing agent work with a senior beside them, owning one small system end to end, and writing the specs and tests the agents build from. Writing those specs and tests is a real job. It might turn out to be the job.

Five guesses for 2031

Okay, now the guessing part. Bookmark this page and come back in 2031 to laugh at me.

Teams get smaller, and there are a lot more of them. According to Y Combinator’s Jared Friedman, a quarter of the Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were about 95% AI-generated. In February, Block cut about 4,000 jobs, and Jack Dorsey pointed to AI tools and “smaller and flatter teams.” I could be wrong here, but I still don’t think that adds up to fewer software jobs overall, and neither does the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, which projects 10% growth for software developers, QA analysts and testers from 2025 to 2035.

When something gets cheaper, we tend to want more of it. Economists call this the Jevons paradox, after William Stanley Jevons, who argued in 1865 that more efficient steam engines would make Britain burn more coal. Software that took a team a quarter will take one person a week, and a lot of problems nobody could afford to solve will suddenly be worth solving.

The spec and the tests become the source. Today we treat the code as the thing we own and the spec as the document nobody reads. I think that flips. The spec and the tests become what you review and argue about, and the code becomes more like a compiler’s output: you can open it and inspect it, but you rarely edit it by hand. (Yes, that’s the 1954 promise again. Maybe this time it sticks.)

Software for an audience of one. My nightly agent builds things nobody asked for, including me, and some of them are delightful. When a working tool costs an evening instead of a quarter, people will make software the way they make spreadsheets today: for one problem and one person, thrown away when it’s done.

Reading code becomes a career. We have whole careers built around writing code and almost none built around reading it. I expect that to change, with something like “verification engineer” on job boards and much better tooling that shows a reviewer the recording, the risky lines and the tests the agent didn’t write. The Faros numbers say we need it now, never mind in 2031.

Every change carries a label. I think a pull request will routinely say who or what wrote it, who checked it, and what was actually verified. I already do a small version of this: every project my nightly agent builds says so, in its README and on this site.

Back to Tuesday

FORTRAN did eliminate a kind of coding. It didn’t eliminate coders. It made a lot more of them, working on harder problems, and the debugging came along for the ride.

I think AI does the same thing, faster and messier. The developer of 2031 spends the day deciding what should exist, explaining it clearly enough that a machine can build it, and checking that what came back is right. That was always the hard part. We just had less time for it because we were busy typing.

What does your Tuesday look like right now? Are you reviewing more than you write? Tell me in the comments. I’d like to know if my guess is already wrong.

That build is now Rule Safari, a live project on this site, with an article explaining how it works.
So is this the end of programming? People have been asking that for more than seventy years. I find that comforting. I also find it a little suspicious.
Programming has been ending since 1954

On 10 November 1954, IBM’s Programming Research Group finished a preliminary report on a new language called FORTRAN. One sentence in it says that FORTRAN “should virtually eliminate coding and debugging.”

I love this sentence. It’s so sure of itself, and it even came with a budget: problems solved “for less than half the cost” of doing it without FORTRAN. The industry had a name for this kind of thing back then. Assemblers and compilers were called automatic programming. You’d describe what you wanted, and the machine would write the program.

FORTRAN shipped in 1957, and it really did eliminate a kind of coding. Almost nobody translates formulas into machine instructions by hand anymore. Debugging survived just fine. (This month I chased a Scry bug that came down to a bookmark saved only every twelve hours, so I can confirm debugging is alive and well.)

What FORTRAN actually did was take one tedious part of the job away and move the job up a level. People stopped thinking about registers and started thinking about bigger problems. Programs got cheaper to write, so everybody wanted more of them. That has happened over and over since.
Assembly languageYou stopped: writing instructions as raw numbersKathleen Booth, "Coding for A.R.C."
FORTRANYou stopped: translating formulas into machine instructions by handThe 1954 report: it "should virtually eliminate coding and debugging."
CYou stopped: rewriting the same program for every new machine
The Last OneYou stopped: nothing, as it turned outA BASIC program generator, named as the last program you would ever need to buy.
Stack OverflowYou stopped: solving every error message alone
npmYou stopped: writing your own everything
GitHub CopilotYou stopped: typing the boilerplate
Coding agentsYou stopped: typing most of the code
NextYou stopped: ?

My favorite rung is 1981. A British company called D.J. “AI” Systems (yes, really) sold a BASIC program generator named The Last One. The name was the whole pitch. It would write all your programs for you, so it would be the last program you’d ever need to buy.
Reviewers found it useful for some business programs. It was not the last one.

Here’s the pattern on every rung. Something gets automated, the people doing the work stop doing that thing by hand, and the field keeps growing anyway. GitHub counted more than 180 million developers in its 2025 report, and more than 36 million of them had joined in the previous twelve months.

So I don’t think AI ends programming. I do think this rung is different in one way, and that’s speed. GitHub Copilot’s preview came out in June 2021. By 2025, 84% of developers in Stack Overflow’s survey were using AI tools or planning to. Four years, from novelty to default.
What 2026 actually looks like

The vibes are loud right now, so let’s start with numbers. (Speaking of vibes: Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” in February 2025, for the kind of coding where you “fully give in to the vibes.” Stack Overflow asked about it that year. 72% of developers said it isn’t part of their professional work, and another 5% said emphatically no. I love that they offered that option.)

Stack Overflow’s survey is the biggest regular check-up we have, and the adoption curve in it is steep: from 70% of developers using AI tools or planning to in 2023, to 84% in 2025, when half of professional developers were using them every day.

You’d think all that use would mean developers love these tools. Nope. Favorable sentiment fell from 77% in 2023 to 60% in 2025, and only ticked back up to 62% this year. In 2025, more developers distrusted the accuracy of AI output (46%) than trusted it (33%). The top frustration, picked by 66% of them, was “AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite.”
I feel seen. Almost right is an expensive kind of wrong, because you have to read every line to find the part that isn’t. (45% of them said debugging AI-generated code takes longer.)

Then there’s my favorite study of the whole AI boom, mostly because it’s so rude. In early 2025, METR, a nonprofit research group, ran a proper randomized controlled trial. Sixteen experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real issues in their own repositories, projects they’d been on for years, and each issue was randomly assigned to allow AI tools or ban them.
Before they started, the developers expected AI to cut their time by 24%. When they finished, they believed it had cut it by 20%. The clock said that with AI they took 19% longer.
Nineteen percent longer! And they walked away sure it had helped.
← longershorter →
Economists predictedexpert forecast39% less time
ML researchers predictedexpert forecast38% less time
The developers expectedbefore the tasks24% less time
The developers feltafter the tasks20% less time
The clock measuredwhat happened19% more time
Before anyone screenshots that for a hot take: it’s one study of sixteen people, using early-2025 tools, on codebases they knew better than any model could.

And METR tried to run it again. A bigger study started in August 2025, with 57 developers and more than 800 tasks, and in February 2026 METR said the data was too unreliable to lean on. Mostly that was because developers kept declining to take part, since they “do not wish to work without AI.” The early numbers hinted at an 18% speedup for the returning developers (with a range wide enough to include no speedup at all).
I think that’s the most 2026 way an experiment has ever failed. People refused to be in the group without AI.

What I take from METR is narrower than any headline, and more useful: how fast you feel is not a measurement. If you want to know whether AI makes your team faster, measure it the way you’d measure anything else.
The line that keeps going up

METR’s other big project tracks how long a task an AI agent can finish on its own. They time human experts on a suite of software tasks, then find the task length where an agent succeeds half the time. In 2019, GPT-2 managed tasks that take a person about three seconds. GPT-4 got to about four minutes in 2023. Claude 3.7 Sonnet reached an hour in February 2025, and Claude Opus 4.6 reached about twelve hours a year later.
Across the whole series, that number has doubled about every six months. Since 2023, it’s been closer to every four months.
1 min1 hour1 workday1 work week1 work month2019202120232025202720292031if the trend holdsGPT-2GPT-4Claude 3.7 SonnetGPT-5Claude Opus 4.6

Now, a log-scale chart with a dashed line on the end is how a lot of bad predictions start, so let me be careful. “Half the time” is doing a lot of work in that definition. Benchmark tasks are cleaner than your codebase. And METR stopped updating that page in September. But if the line keeps going even roughly, agents will handle a month of human work, half the time, around 2028. That’s where my 2031 Tuesday comes from. I didn’t pull it out of thin air. I pulled it out of a log-scale chart, which is thin air with axes.

The companies building these things are already living a version of it. Google said in October 2024 that more than a quarter of its new code was generated by AI, and “well over 30%” six months later. In March 2025, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei predicted AI would be writing 90% of code within three to six months. That was too soon. But by May 2026, Anthropic said more than 80% of the code merged into its own codebase was written by Claude.
When code gets cheap, the queue moves

Make one step of a process faster and the work piles up in front of the next slowest step. Anyone who has worked a kitchen on a Saturday night knows this: speed up the grill and the plates start waiting at the pass.

That’s what’s happening to software teams. In 2025, Faros AI looked at telemetry from more than 10,000 developers on 1,255 teams. Developers on teams with high AI adoption finished 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests, and their review time went up 91%.

Faros ran it again in 2026 with 22,000 developers. Task completion per developer was up 34%, which sounds great until you read the rest. Median review time had grown five times. 31% more pull requests were merging without any review at all, and the ratio of incidents to pull requests had more than tripled.

The code got cheaper, the reading got more expensive, and some teams quietly stopped reading. That matters because the code isn’t always good. Veracode tested more than 100 language models on 80 coding tasks in 2025, and 45% of the results had a security flaw. GitClear found that copy-pasted lines went from 8.3% of changed code in 2021 to 12.3% in 2024, while moved code, the kind you get from refactoring, fell from about a quarter to under 10%.

Spare a thought for the maintainers, too. Daniel Stenberg, who leads curl, started banning people who submitted “AI slop” bug reports in May 2025, writing that the project was “effectively being DDoSed.” In January 2026, curl shut down its bug bounty.
Decide what to build
Write it down
Write the code
Review it
Check it works
Ship and run it
Today: code arrives faster than people can read it, so pull requests wait for review.

Fred Brooks saw a version of this coming in 1986. In “No Silver Bullet” he split the difficulties of software into two piles, borrowing Aristotle’s words: essence and accidents. The accidents are the trouble our tools cause us, like syntax, boilerplate and fighting the build. The essence is what he called “the specification, design, and testing of this conceptual construct,” which is a fancy way of saying: working out what the thing should do. AI is getting very good at the accidents. The essence is the refund question from 2:13 a.m., and it’s still on your desk.
The rung we might be sawing off
This is the part of the data I like least.

In August 2025, Erik Brynjolfsson and two colleagues at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab used ADP payroll data to look at who was getting hired. Employment for software developers aged 22 to 25 was down nearly 20% from its peak in late 2022. Older developers showed no noticeable change.

They updated the study this August, with data through June 2026. Young workers in AI-exposed jobs are now 19% below where they’d be if they had kept pace with less-exposed peers. Experienced workers show no comparable gap. Most of the effect comes from companies hiring fewer young people in the first place.
The rest of the market isn’t exactly roaring either. Indeed’s index of software development job postings sits about 21% below February 2020, after bottoming out 39% below in May 2025.

The Stanford authors are careful to call their findings descriptive, not causal, and plenty else has happened since 2022. Interest rates went up, and a lot of companies had hired too many people during the pandemic (Indeed’s index peaked at more than twice its 2020 level in early 2022). But the pattern lines up uncomfortably well with what agents are good at: the small, well-defined ticket we used to give the new person on the team.

Senior engineers get made on the job, mostly by being juniors on real teams: doing the boring tickets, breaking production once, and having someone kind explain why. If agents take all the boring tickets, where does the next senior engineer come from? It’s hard to review code well if you’ve never written much of it.

I don’t have a clean answer. My guess is that the teams doing well in 2035 will be the ones that kept hiring juniors in 2026 and gave them a different apprenticeship: reviewing agent work with a senior beside them, owning one small system end to end, and writing the specs and tests the agents build from. Writing those specs and tests is a real job. It might turn out to be the job.
Five guesses for 2031
Okay, now the guessing part. Bookmark this page and come back in 2031 to laugh at me.

Teams get smaller, and there are a lot more of them. According to Y Combinator’s Jared Friedman, a quarter of the Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were about 95% AI-generated. In February, Block cut about 4,000 jobs, and Jack Dorsey pointed to AI tools and “smaller and flatter teams.” I could be wrong here, but I still don’t think that adds up to fewer software jobs overall, and neither does the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, which projects 10% growth for software developers, QA analysts and testers from 2025 to 2035.

When something gets cheaper, we tend to want more of it. Economists call this the Jevons paradox, after William Stanley Jevons, who argued in 1865 that more efficient steam engines would make Britain burn more coal. Software that took a team a quarter will take one person a week, and a lot of problems nobody could afford to solve will suddenly be worth solving.

The spec and the tests become the source. Today we treat the code as the thing we own and the spec as the document nobody reads. I think that flips. The spec and the tests become what you review and argue about, and the code becomes more like a compiler’s output: you can open it and inspect it, but you rarely edit it by hand. (Yes, that’s the 1954 promise again. Maybe this time it sticks.)

Software for an audience of one. My nightly agent builds things nobody asked for, including me, and some of them are delightful. When a working tool costs an evening instead of a quarter, people will make software the way they make spreadsheets today: for one problem and one person, thrown away when it’s done.

Reading code becomes a career. We have whole careers built around writing code and almost none built around reading it. I expect that to change, with something like “verification engineer” on job boards and much better tooling that shows a reviewer the recording, the risky lines and the tests the agent didn’t write. The Faros numbers say we need it now, never mind in 2031.

Every change carries a label. I think a pull request will routinely say who or what wrote it, who checked it, and what was actually verified. I already do a small version of this: every project my nightly agent builds says so, in its README and on this site.
Back to Tuesday
FORTRAN did eliminate a kind of coding. It didn’t eliminate coders. It made a lot more of them, working on harder problems, and the debugging came along for the ride.

I think AI does the same thing, faster and messier. The developer of 2031 spends the day deciding what should exist, explaining it clearly enough that a machine can build it, and checking that what came back is right. That was always the hard part. We just had less time for it because we were busy typing.
What does your Tuesday look like right now? Are you reviewing more than you write? Tell me in the comments. I’d like to know if my guess is already wrong.

The open-source managed agent platform A self-hostable alternative to Claude Managed Agents and OpenAI's Agents API. Website · Quickstart · Docs · API · Changelog · Discord Omnara is an open-source managed agent platform. Use the API to run AI agents on any model and any machine, with tools, secrets, permissions, and streaming built in. Self-host it for free under Apache 2.0, or use Omnara Cloud. Sign in at app.omnara.com. Your first project comes with a model provider (omnara-openrouter) and a pool of managed sandboxes (default-pool), so this config runs as is. Save it as agent.yaml: version: v1 instruction: | You are an engineering assistant. Use your machine to run commands. model: provider_config: omnara-openrouter name: anthropic/claude-fable-5.1 machine_sources: - machine_pool_name: default-pool Launch it with the CLI (Node.js 22 or newer). If you're not logged in, the first command opens your browser to sign in. npx omnara agents launch --file agent.yaml \ --name "Machine assistant" \ --message "Report this machine's operating system and free disk space." Chat with the agent in your terminal with npx omnara agents chat , or open it in the dashboard to watch its tool calls and reply. Create an API key in the dashboard and export it as OMNARA_TOKEN, install the SDK with npm install @omnara/sdk, and use the org and project IDs that npx omnara config prints: import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises' import { bearerToken, createOmnaraClient, openAgentEventStream, sdk } from '@omnara/sdk' const client = createOmnaraClient({ auth: bearerToken(process.env.OMNARA_TOKEN!) }) const path = { orgID: 'org_...', projectID: 'proj_...' } const config = await sdk.createAgentConfig({ client, path, body: { source: await readFile('agent.yaml', 'utf8'), source_format: 'yaml' }, }) const launched = await sdk.createAgent({ client, path, body: { config: config.data.id, message: "Report this machine's free disk space." }, }) const agentID = launched.data.agent.id for await (const event of openAgentEventStream({ client, path: { ...path, agentID } })) { console.log(event) } The quickstart shows the same flow with the REST API. To have your coding agent do the setup, give it this prompt: Help me set up Omnara by following https://www.omnara.com/SKILL.md Requires Docker with Compose. git clone https://github.com/omnara-ai/omnara.git cd omnara docker compose -f compose.yaml --profile app up -d Open http://localhost:8000 and sign up. Local development prints the verification link in docker compose logs api, so no email provider is needed. To build from source instead of using published images, run docker compose --profile app up -d --build. A new instance has no models or machines yet. In the console, add a model provider and a model, connect this computer under Machines, and share both with your project. Sandboxes also work once your instance has a public URL. Point the CLI at your instance and log in: npx omnara config --api-url http://localhost:8000/api/v1 --issuer-url http://localhost:8000 npx omnara login In agent.yaml, use your provider and model names, and replace the machine_pool_name entry with machine_name: . Then launch it with the same command as above. The local defaults are intentionally insecure. For a real deployment, follow the self-hosting guide and the configuration reference. Your product talks to Omnara, and Omnara runs each agent with the model, tools, and machines in its config. flowchart TB subgraph yours["Your side"] users(["Your users"]) --> app["Your app
REST API · TypeScript SDK"] team["Your team
CLI · dashboard
Slack · Discord · GitHub"] end subgraph omnara["Omnara"] api["API
launch · input
event stream · approvals"] <--> pg[("Postgres
each agent's event log")] <--> worker["Workers
run the agent loop"] end subgraph plug[" "] models["Models
OpenAI · Anthropic
OpenRouter · self-hosted"] tools["Tools
built-in · skills
MCP · custom"] machines["Machines
sandboxes or your own
laptop, VM, container"] end app --> api team --> api worker --> models worker --> tools worker --> machines classDef side fill:none,stroke:#8b949e,stroke-width:1px classDef core fill:#506FCF,stroke:#3D5BB5,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff classDef store fill:#3D5BB5,stroke:#2E4794,stroke-width:1px,color:#ffffff classDef plugin fill:none,stroke:#85A0E6,stroke-width:1.5px class users,app,team side class api,worker core class pg store class models,tools,machines plugin style yours fill:none,stroke:#8b949e,stroke-dasharray:4 3 style omnara fill:#506FCF14,stroke:#506FCF,stroke-width:1.5px style plug fill:none,stroke:#85A0E6,stroke-dasharray:4 3 linkStyle default stroke:#8b949e,stroke-width:1.5px Loading API. Your app, the CLI, and the dashboard all use the same REST API to launch agents, send messages, and answer approvals. Events stream back as they happen. Postgres. Every step of every agent is saved here. That record is the agent's state, so any worker can pick an agent back up after a crash or restart. Workers. Stateless processes that build the model context, call the model, and run tools. An agent only uses a worker while it's taking a turn, so one worker can serve many agents. Add workers to handle more turns at once. Machines. Each machine runs the omnarad daemon, which connects out to Omnara, so agents can run commands there without any inbound ports. Omnara also uses Redis, blob storage for attachments and tool outputs, and a memory filesystem. The architecture docs cover the details. Any model. Bring your own keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Amazon Bedrock, LiteLLM, Ollama, or any compatible endpoint, including models you host yourself. Tools. Built-in tools for shell commands, files, web search and fetch, and asking a person a question, plus MCP servers and custom tools that run in your own systems. Skills. Package instructions and files once, attach them to any agent, and the agent loads them when it needs them. Memory. Memory stores give agents files that persist between conversations and can be shared with other agents, with read or read-write access per agent. Subagents. An agent can start subagents with a fresh context, check their progress, and send them new instructions. Each subagent is a full agent you can inspect. Machines. Machines are tools the agent uses. Install the Omnara daemon on any macOS or Linux laptop, VM, or container and your agents can run commands and edit files there, with no inbound ports or SSH keys. Or use sandboxes from eleven providers (Arker, Blaxel, boxd, CreateOS, Daytona, E2B, Freestyle, Modal, Superserve, Tenki, Unikraft). An agent can use several machines at once (for example, a set of GPU servers) and move between them. If your laptop goes offline, the agent can continue in a sandbox and sync its work back with git. Durable state. Every step is saved, so agents pick up where they left off after crashes, restarts, and machine disconnects. Schedules. Cron triggers with time zones can message an existing agent, launch a new one from a profile, or start a new Slack or Discord thread. Slack, Discord, and GitHub. Mention the bot in Slack or Discord to start an agent in a thread, where it replies, asks questions, and requests approvals. On GitHub, an agent can start when a pull request opens or someone mentions it, then read the diff, comment, and submit reviews. To connect another service, build a custom integration on the same public API. Streaming and webhooks. Stream every event as it happens or receive it as a webhook, and send new messages while the agent works. Permissions. Each tool can run immediately, ask a person first, or be blocked. The platform enforces the setting, and the agent waits until someone approves or denies the call. API, SDK, and CLI. A REST API defined in api/openapi/openapi.yaml, a TypeScript SDK (@omnara/sdk), a CLI (omnara), and an MCP server. Role-based access control and secrets. Organization and project roles for users and API keys. Credentials for models, machines, and MCP servers are stored once and shared with each project explicitly. Multi-tenant. One deployment serves many organizations, each with its own members, projects, secrets, model providers, and machines. Self-hosted operators can give every new organization default models and sandboxes, as Omnara Cloud does. Your data. Self-hosted deployments keep every agent's history in your own Postgres, where you can query it for analytics, evals, and training datasets. Omnara vs Claude Managed Agents and OpenAI's Agents API Claude Managed Agents and OpenAI's Agents API are hosted services for running agents on one company's models. Omnara does the same job as an open-source platform you can run anywhere, with any model. Omnara Claude Managed Agents OpenAI's Agents API Source Open source (Apache 2.0) Closed Open-source harness (Codex). The hosted service is OpenAI's. Models Any compatible model Claude OpenAI Agent loop Omnara's, works with any model Anthropic's, built for Claude Codex, run and updated by OpenAI Where the platform runs Omnara Cloud, or your own infrastructure Anthropic's cloud OpenAI's cloud Where agents run Sandboxes from many providers, or your own machines Anthropic sandboxes, or your own sandboxes OpenAI sandboxes, partner sandboxes, or your own machines Operations Managed on Omnara Cloud. You operate it when self-hosting. Managed by Anthropic. You run the sandbox side if you self-host sandboxes. Managed by OpenAI. You run the environment if you bring your own. Agent history Stored by Omnara on Omnara Cloud and queryable through the API. In your own Postgres when self-hosted. Stored by Anthropic, readable and deletable through the API. Not currently eligible for Zero Data Retention or HIPAA BAA coverage. Stored by OpenAI. No Zero Data Retention support. US data residency only. Pricing Free to self-host. On Omnara Cloud, free with your own keys and machines, or pay as you go for our models and sandboxes. Claude token rates plus $0.08 per active session-hour OpenAI model rates, plus standard rates for OpenAI tools and hosted sandboxes Choose Claude Managed Agents or the Agents API if you use one company's models and want that company to run everything for you. Choose Omnara if you want to pick your models and machines, run the platform yourself, or keep agent data in your own database. If you use It's good for Omnara adds Workflow builders, such as n8n or Zapier Predictable, step-by-step automations Open-ended agents that run code on machines and keep state for days Agent frameworks, such as Mastra, LangChain, or the OpenAI Agents SDK Agent logic in your app's code Hosting, state, machines, permissions, and integrations, with agents created and changed through an API instead of a redeploy Agent harnesses, such as Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK, Codex, OpenCode, or Pi One agent loop in a terminal or on one machine Cloud agents that run as a service, across machines and users, started from your app, Slack, GitHub, or a schedule Managed agent platforms, such as Claude Managed Agents or the Agents API Hosted agents on one company's models The same model of hosted agents, open source, on any model, and self-hostable Each of these is an agent.yaml plus a SKILL.md in examples/, and you can deploy any of them with one prompt to your coding agent. Slack coding agent fixes issues you mention in Slack, Discord, or a GitHub pull request and opens a PR. PR review agent reviews your GitHub pull requests against a checkout of the repository and leaves inline findings. SRE agent investigates production problems such as a 5xx spike. Browser agent works in a real browser on long-running tasks. PostHog analytics agent compares yesterday's product usage with the 7-day average and reports what changed. Reddit, X, and LinkedIn signal agents summarize the last 24 hours of posts about a topic you pick. Video generation agent makes short videos from a brief. There are also code samples for a CLI chat app built on the TypeScript SDK, custom tools over webhooks, and a SharePoint filesystem mount. Use Omnara from your coding agent MCP server. Connect Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any MCP client that supports OAuth to https://app.omnara.com/mcp to launch and manage Omnara agents. You sign in through the browser, so there are no tokens to paste. In Claude, add it from the connectors directory. Omnara is also listed in the official MCP Registry as com.omnara/omnara. claude mcp add --transport http omnara https://app.omnara.com/mcp codex mcp add omnara --url https://app.omnara.com/mcp Then sign in with /mcp in Claude Code or codex mcp login omnara in Codex. See Connecting MCP clients. CLI. omnara manages agents, profiles, machines, model providers, secrets, skills, and cron triggers from your terminal or your coding agent's shell. Run npx omnara --help to start. Setup skill. skills/setup-omnara-agent, also served at omnara.com/SKILL.md, walks a coding agent through setting up Omnara for your project. Docs for LLMs. docs.omnara.com/llms.txt. What is Omnara? An open-source managed agent platform for running AI agents on any model and any machine. How much does it cost? Nothing to self-host. Omnara Cloud has no platform fee. You can bring your own model keys and machines for free, or pay as you go for our models at provider token rates and our sandboxes by active time and retained storage. See pricing. Can I self-host it? Yes. Run it with Docker Compose locally, then follow the self-hosting guide for production. The API, CLI, SDK, and config format are the same on Omnara Cloud and self-hosted deployments. Which models work? Any model behind an OpenAI Responses, OpenAI Chat Completions, or Anthropic Messages compatible endpoint, including OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Amazon Bedrock, LiteLLM, and Ollama. Source development requires the Go version declared in go.mod, Node.js 24 or newer with Corepack, ripgrep, and Docker with Compose. Run the fast repository gate with make verify. See CONTRIBUTING.md for the full test suite, generated-code workflows, and pull request expectations. Discord · GitHub Issues · X · Security Apache License 2.0 Launch it from your code with the TypeScript SDK

public URL.
Point the CLI at your instance and log in:

npx omnara config --api-url http://localhost:8000/api/v1 --issuer-url http://localhost:8000
npx omnara login

In agent.yaml, use your provider and model names, and replace the
machine_pool_name entry with machine_name: <your machine>. Then launch it
with the same command as above.

The local defaults are intentionally insecure. For a real deployment, follow
the self-hosting guide and
the configuration reference.

Your product talks to Omnara, and Omnara runs each agent with the model,
tools, and machines in its config.

Loading

API. Your app, the CLI, and the dashboard all use the same REST API to
launch agents, send messages, and answer approvals. Events stream back as
they happen.

Postgres. Every step of every agent is saved here. That record is the
agent's state, so any worker can pick an agent back up after a crash or
restart.

Workers. Stateless processes that build the model context, call the
model, and run tools. An agent only uses a worker while it's taking a turn,
so one worker can serve many agents. Add workers to handle more turns at
once.

Machines. Each machine runs the omnarad daemon, which connects out to
Omnara, so agents can run commands there without any inbound ports.

Omnara also uses Redis, blob storage for attachments and tool outputs, and a
memory filesystem. The
architecture docs cover the details.

Any model. Bring
your own keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Amazon Bedrock, LiteLLM,
Ollama, or any compatible endpoint, including models you host yourself.

Tools. Built-in tools for shell
commands, files, web search and fetch, and asking a person a question, plus
MCP servers and
custom tools that run in your own
systems.

Skills. Package instructions and
files once, attach them to any agent, and the agent loads them when it needs
them.

Memory.
Memory stores give agents files that persist between conversations and can
be shared with other agents, with read or read-write access per agent.

Subagents. An agent
can start subagents with a fresh context, check their progress, and send them
new instructions. Each subagent is a full agent you can inspect.

Machines. Machines are tools
the agent uses. Install the Omnara daemon on any macOS or Linux laptop, VM, or
container and your agents can run commands and edit files there, with no inbound ports or
SSH keys. Or use sandboxes from eleven providers (Arker, Blaxel, boxd, CreateOS,
Daytona, E2B, Freestyle, Modal, Superserve, Tenki, Unikraft). An agent can use several machines
at once (for example, a set of GPU servers) and move between them. If your
laptop goes offline, the agent can continue in a sandbox and sync its work
back with git.

Durable state. Every step is
saved, so agents pick up where they left off after crashes, restarts, and
machine disconnects.

Schedules.
Cron triggers with time zones can message an existing agent, launch a new one
from a profile, or
start a new Slack or Discord thread.

Slack, Discord, and GitHub.
Mention the bot in Slack or Discord to start an agent in a thread, where it
replies, asks questions, and requests approvals. On GitHub, an agent can start
when a pull request opens or someone mentions it, then read the diff,
comment, and submit reviews. To connect another service, build a
custom integration
on the same public API.

Streaming and
webhooks. Stream every event as
it happens or receive it as a webhook, and send new messages while the agent
works.

Permissions. Each tool can
run immediately, ask a person first, or be blocked. The platform enforces the
setting, and the agent waits until someone approves or denies the call.

API, SDK, and CLI. A REST API
defined in api/openapi/openapi.yaml, a
TypeScript SDK (@omnara/sdk),
a CLI (omnara), and an MCP server.

Role-based access control
and secrets. Organization
and project roles for users and API keys. Credentials for
models, machines, and MCP servers are stored once and shared with each
project explicitly.

Multi-tenant. One deployment serves
many organizations, each with its own members, projects, secrets, model
providers, and machines. Self-hosted operators can give every new
organization default models and sandboxes, as Omnara Cloud does.

Your data. Self-hosted deployments keep every agent's history in your own
Postgres, where you can query it for analytics, evals, and training datasets.
Omnara vs Claude Managed Agents and OpenAI's Agents API

Claude Managed Agents
and OpenAI's Agents API
are hosted services for running agents on one company's models. Omnara does the
same job as an open-source platform you can run anywhere, with any model.

Operations

Pricing
Free to self-host. On Omnara Cloud, free with your own keys and machines, or pay as you go for our models and sandboxes.

Choose Claude Managed Agents or the Agents API if you use one company's models
and want that company to run everything for you. Choose Omnara if you want to
pick your models and machines, run the platform yourself, or keep agent data in
your own database.

Omnara adds
Workflow builders, such as n8n or Zapier

Each of these is an agent.yaml plus a SKILL.md in examples/,
and you can deploy any of them with one prompt to your coding agent.

Slack coding agent fixes issues you mention in
Slack, Discord, or a GitHub pull request and opens a PR.

PR review agent reviews your GitHub pull requests
against a checkout of the repository and leaves inline findings.

SRE agent investigates production problems such as a
5xx spike.

Browser agent works in a real browser on
long-running tasks.

PostHog analytics agent compares
yesterday's product usage with the 7-day average and reports what changed.

Reddit, X, and
LinkedIn signal agents summarize the last
24 hours of posts about a topic you pick.

Video generation agent makes short videos
from a brief.

There are also code samples for a CLI chat app built on
the TypeScript SDK, custom tools over webhooks,
and a SharePoint filesystem mount.
Use Omnara from your coding agent

MCP server. Connect Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any MCP client that
supports OAuth to https://app.omnara.com/mcp to launch and manage Omnara
agents. You sign in through the browser, so there are no tokens to paste. In
Claude, add it from the
connectors directory. Omnara is
also listed in the official MCP Registry as com.omnara/omnara.

claude mcp add --transport http omnara https://app.omnara.com/mcp
codex mcp add omnara --url https://app.omnara.com/mcp

Then sign in with /mcp in Claude Code or codex mcp login omnara in Codex.
See Connecting MCP clients.

CLI. omnara manages agents,
profiles, machines, model providers, secrets, skills, and cron triggers from
your terminal or your coding agent's shell. Run npx omnara --help to start.

Setup skill. skills/setup-omnara-agent,
also served at omnara.com/SKILL.md, walks a
coding agent through setting up Omnara for your project.
Docs for LLMs. docs.omnara.com/llms.txt.

What is Omnara? An open-source managed agent platform for running AI agents
on any model and any machine.

How much does it cost? Nothing to self-host. Omnara Cloud has no platform
fee. You can bring your own model keys and machines for free, or pay as you go
for our models at provider token rates and our sandboxes by active time and
retained storage. See pricing.

Can I self-host it? Yes. Run it with Docker Compose locally, then follow
the self-hosting guide for
production. The API, CLI, SDK, and config format are the same on Omnara Cloud
and self-hosted deployments.

Which models work? Any model behind an OpenAI Responses, OpenAI Chat
Completions, or Anthropic Messages compatible endpoint, including OpenAI,
Anthropic, OpenRouter, Amazon Bedrock, LiteLLM, and Ollama.

Source development requires the Go version declared in go.mod,
Node.js 24 or newer with Corepack, ripgrep, and Docker with Compose. Run the
fast repository gate with make verify. See CONTRIBUTING.md
for the full test suite, generated-code workflows, and pull request
expectations.

items.text:
155 款应用拒绝豆包助手 AI 自动化操作


10 月 14 日，豆包手机助手《屏幕自动化操作声明协议》（SAEP）30 天公示期结束，官方公布名单显示，已有 155 款第三方应用拒绝 AI 自动化操作，腾讯、阿里、美团、快手旗下多款产品，连同 Kimi、DeepSeek 等 AI 产品均在名单内，堪称互联网头部厂商的集体表态。


SAEP 协议核心是将 AI 屏幕自动操作的选择权交还应用开发者，开发者可自主决定是否允许豆包助手执行屏幕识别、模拟点击等操作。公示期内应用默认不开放权限；公示结束后，未明确拒绝的应用将按风险分级逐步开放，拒绝方后续也可随时调整声明。该自动化权限仅影响 AI 代操作，不影响用户手动使用 App。


此前，努比亚 NaviX Ultra 搭载豆包手机助手发售，就出现过设备触发游戏风控等冲突，这类矛盾过去长期处于隐性博弈状态。本次拒绝名单基本集中在拥有独立流量闭环的平台，安全风险、流量主权是核心考量。SAEP 把隐性冲突转为公开规则协商，标志移动端 AI 入口权博弈正式开启。行业认为，这只是智能体时代生态确权的起点，后续权限细化、责任划分、利益分配仍需多方持续磨合。（来源：极客公园）


相关报道：第一款 AI 手机，被半个互联网「拒」了

腾讯上线绿泡泡短剧


近日，腾讯低调上线绿泡泡短剧，主打「免费好剧，一点就看」。

绿泡泡的界面分为「免费剧场」「刷一刷」和「我的」三部分。「免费剧场」下设「AI 剧」「真人剧」「每日上新」「动漫剧」「本周必看」「百万播放」等栏目。点开中间入口「刷一刷」，上下滑动即进入沉浸式推荐流。剧集全部免费，但会在剧集之间插入广告。


《短剧小程序用户协议》显示，服务签订主体为深圳市腾讯计算机系统有限公司。协议同时写明，短剧均来自第三方提供方，包括第三方小程序、短剧制作方、授权发行方等，由其授权本服务展示、播放。


和红果短剧相比，绿泡泡的社交印记更重。除了常规排行榜，首页还有「朋友在看」的短剧推荐，以及标注「北京的朋友都在看」的地区热门榜。腾讯方面表示，为提供个性化内容，会收集用户的浏览、观看、分享、点赞、评论、收藏等记录，以及朋友看过的剧目。经过程序分析后，平台会预测用户的偏好，朋友在看什么，直接影响给相关用户推什么。


这并非腾讯首次下场做短剧。2021 年 12 月，腾讯视频发布业内首个微短剧品牌「十分剧场」，当时它只是长视频 App 里的一个频道页。2025 年 1 月，「火星短剧社」在微信上线，后改名「火星观剧」，是腾讯首款独立短剧产品。2025 年 6 月，微信上线名为「短剧」的官方小程序。到 2026 年 10 月，这个小程序已找不到入口，位置让给了绿泡泡。（来源：北京日报）

小鹏发布智能汽车解决方案业务


2026 巴黎国际车展期间，小鹏集团董事长兼 CEO 何小鹏作为巴黎汽车峰会唯一受邀的中国车企 CEO，发表重要演讲。何小鹏向与会的行业高管、全球媒体等，正式介绍其智能汽车解决方案业务：「XPENG AI ENGINEERING」，小鹏将面向全球合作伙伴开放智能汽车技术合作，输出覆盖整车研发、生产到售后的一站式能力。并将开放涵盖机器人、Robotaxi、飞行汽车、图灵 AI 芯片、物理世界基座模型等物理 AI 生态全领域的技术合作方案。


何小鹏表示：「开放已经成为小鹏与全球伙伴深化合作的关键词。我们不仅与合作伙伴共享技术，更与合作伙伴共同成长，全力支持合作伙伴掌握技术、开展自主创新。我们也欢迎全球合作伙伴加入，让我们互通技术、互学共进、携手前行」。（来源：新浪科技）

比亚迪欧洲建厂计划披露：法国候选


日前，比亚迪执行副总裁李柯在 2026 巴黎车展上表示，比亚迪将在欧洲大规模投资制造，比亚迪匈牙利工厂计划在今年第四季度启动大规模生产。


同时，比亚迪也将在欧洲建立第二、第三工厂。目前，法国已进入比亚迪欧洲建厂的候选名单。（来源：第一财经）

消息称 Anthropic 第三季度营收达 168 亿美元，已实现调整后盈利


10 月 15 日消息，据彭博社报道，知情人士透露，人工智能模型企业 Anthropic PBC 向潜在投资者表示，公司第三季度营收达到 168 亿美元，这家企业正继续推进上市计划。


知情人士称，开发 Claude 的 Anthropic 于当地时间周三在旧金山总部举办了推介会，向投资者说明，公司在该季度实现了调整后盈利。


知情人士表示，截至第三季度，Anthropic 已经实现正向自由现金流，调整后毛利率为 85%，调整后营业利润率超过 11%。


Anthropic 预计最早在 11 月 9 日那一周正式启动首次公开募股的路演工作，有望在感恩节前挂牌交易，预计年内完成上市。


知情人士表示，相关讨论仍在进行，时间安排仍有可能变动。（来源：IT 之家）

千问办公发布电商版，开启邀测


10 月 14 日，千问办公发布千问办公电商版，基于电商行业商家的日常工作场景进行了 AI 能力的重新设计和增强，尤其是针对跨多平台的电商经营场景，用一个 AI 入口驱动不同的电商平台，帮助商家完成 AI 时代的运营升级。


千问办公电商版已开启邀测，在千问办公中切换至「电商经营」模式即可体验。（来源：新浪科技）


国行 Apple Watch 上线睡眠呼吸暂停迹象提示功能


10 月 14 日消息，今日，苹果宣布在中国大陆推出 Apple Watch「睡眠呼吸暂停通知」功能，Apple 已获得移动睡眠呼吸暂停迹象提示软件由国家药品监督管理局（NMPA）批准的医疗器械注册证。


移动睡眠呼吸暂停迹象提示软件可以在你睡眠期间监测呼吸紊乱，并会在监测到持续性中度到重度睡眠呼吸暂停迹象时通知你。

据悉，该功能早在 2024 年便已登陆部分市场的 Apple Watch，可帮助用户识别中度至重度睡眠呼吸暂停迹象。


具体是如何识别的？苹果官方回应：基于深度学习算法及临床测试数据集构建，利用手表内置的加速感应器监测手腕细微动作以评估正常呼吸节律中断情况。


根据苹果公布的信息，支持该功能的设备包括 Apple Watch Series 9 及后续机型、Apple Watch Ultra 2 及后续机型，以及 Apple Watch SE 3。


具体操作上，将 iPhone 和手表更新至最新系统，打开 iPhone 上的健康 App，在「摘要」中找到「健康核对清单」，下滑最底部找到「移动睡眠呼吸暂停迹象提示软件」，根据指引开通即可。


需要注意的是，开通前需要确保设置过「睡眠」，并打开「通过 Apple Watch 跟踪睡眠」。


开通后，系统每 30 天会对呼吸紊乱数据进行分析。如果数据显示持续存在中度至重度睡眠呼吸暂停的迹象，用户会收到通知。需要注意的是，在为期 30 天的评估期内，必须戴着 Apple Watch 睡至少 10 晚。（来源：TechWeb）

豆包工作支持一键导入 GPT、Claude Code 技能对话，无缝切换


豆包工作正式上线数据导入同步新能力，用户可以一键把 ChatGPT、Claude Code、Trae Work 上面的技能、历史对话、工作记忆迁移过来，实现不同 AI 工具之间无缝切换。（来源：快科技）


会飞的车！特斯拉 Roadster 发布时间定档：马斯克转发预热


特斯拉官宣第二代 Roadster 将于美国时间 10 月 15 日在 SpaceX 测试基地线上直播演示，马斯克也在社交平台转发消息。

这款超跑最早于 2017 年亮相，马斯克曾提出移植 SpaceX 冷气推进技术、布置约 10 个推进器的构想，该构想可优化车辆加速表现、过弯车身姿态甚至实现短暂离地，被外界称为「会飞的跑车」。（来源：快科技）

全球首款 8K 超高清 AI 空间相机：禾赛 Kosmo One 发布，让建模像拍照一样简单


10 月 14 日现场消息，禾赛科技今日发布了「全球首款 8K 超高清 AI 空间相机」——Kosmo One，可将真实世界转化为高质量三维空间模型。

禾赛 Kosmo One 搭载一英寸 CMOS，最高拍摄分辨率可达 8K，实现 360° 无死角覆盖；15 分钟即可完成 100m² 真实空间重建，宣称「让高质量空间建模像拍照一样简单」。


禾赛 Kosmo One 可将真实世界转化为机器人训练数据，用于机器人进行物理 AI 训练，并且可用于世界模型、影视媒体、文旅文化、数字艺术等领域。


禾赛还一同发布了 Kosmo World，这是一个 AI 驱动的云平台，搭配 Kosmo One 可进行一站式 3D 内容创作与管理。（来源：IT 之家）

消息称 Nothing 将推两款智能眼镜：音频版、摄像头版，后者支持 ChatGPT


10 月 14 日消息，据消息人士 Roland Quandt 今日透露，Nothing 将推出两款智能眼镜。其中一款主打音频功能，另一款配备摄像头。

据介绍，Nothing 的音频版智能眼镜支持播放音乐、通话，用户可通过眼镜与手机的语音助手交互。该产品将配备光致变色镜片，可在阳光下自动变暗、室内自动变亮。


同时，该公司还计划推出另一款智能眼镜。该产品将拥有摄像头，支持 ChatGPT、翻译功能。


彭博社此前报道称，Nothing 的智能眼镜将通过手机和云端处理 AI 任务，不会配备 AR 显示屏。（来源：IT 之家）

因《GTA6》规模太大，Rockstar 在美国洛杉矶开设新工作室


10 月 14 日消息，据游戏媒体 Insider Gaming 今天报道，由于《GTA6》游戏规模过于庞大，Rockstar 选择在美国洛杉矶开设新工作室，进一步体现了本作的复杂程度。


R 星开发人员 Rob Nelson 对此表示，当开发团队考虑增加 NPC 数量时，很快就发现已有能力无法满足需求，最终促使公司在洛杉矶设立新工作室。


Rockstar 在洛杉矶工作室聘请了编剧、制作人、导演，专门负责打造 NPC，进一步为玩家打造鲜活、充满生机的世界。


《GTA6》将在 11 月 19 日发售，按照外界预期，《GTA6》有望打破游戏行业的多项纪录。（来源：IT 之家）

blocks.x: 155 款应用拒绝豆包助手 AI 自动化操作
10 月 14 日，豆包手机助手《屏幕自动化操作声明协议》（SAEP）30 天公示期结束，官方公布名单显示，已有 155 款第三方应用拒绝 AI 自动化操作，腾讯、阿里、美团、快手旗下多款产品，连同 Kimi、DeepSeek 等 AI 产品均在名单内，堪称互联网头部厂商的集体表态。
SAEP 协议核心是将 AI 屏幕自动操作的选择权交还应用开发者，开发者可自主决定是否允许豆包助手执行屏幕识别、模拟点击等操作。公示期内应用默认不开放权限；公示结束后，未明确拒绝的应用将按风险分级逐步开放，拒绝方后续也可随时调整声明。该自动化权限仅影响 AI 代操作，不影响用户手动使用 App。
此前，努比亚 NaviX Ultra 搭载豆包手机助手发售，就出现过设备触发游戏风控等冲突，这类矛盾过去长期处于隐性博弈状态。本次拒绝名单基本集中在拥有独立流量闭环的平台，安全风险、流量主权是核心考量。SAEP 把隐性冲突转为公开规则协商，标志移动端 AI 入口权博弈正式开启。行业认为，这只是智能体时代生态确权的起点，后续权限细化、责任划分、利益分配仍需多方持续磨合。（来源：极客公园）
相关报道：第一款 AI 手机，被半个互联网「拒」了
腾讯上线绿泡泡短剧
近日，腾讯低调上线绿泡泡短剧，主打「免费好剧，一点就看」。
绿泡泡的界面分为「免费剧场」「刷一刷」和「我的」三部分。「免费剧场」下设「AI 剧」「真人剧」「每日上新」「动漫剧」「本周必看」「百万播放」等栏目。点开中间入口「刷一刷」，上下滑动即进入沉浸式推荐流。剧集全部免费，但会在剧集之间插入广告。
《短剧小程序用户协议》显示，服务签订主体为深圳市腾讯计算机系统有限公司。协议同时写明，短剧均来自第三方提供方，包括第三方小程序、短剧制作方、授权发行方等，由其授权本服务展示、播放。
和红果短剧相比，绿泡泡的社交印记更重。除了常规排行榜，首页还有「朋友在看」的短剧推荐，以及标注「北京的朋友都在看」的地区热门榜。腾讯方面表示，为提供个性化内容，会收集用户的浏览、观看、分享、点赞、评论、收藏等记录，以及朋友看过的剧目。经过程序分析后，平台会预测用户的偏好，朋友在看什么，直接影响给相关用户推什么。
这并非腾讯首次下场做短剧。2021 年 12 月，腾讯视频发布业内首个微短剧品牌「十分剧场」，当时它只是长视频 App 里的一个频道页。2025 年 1 月，「火星短剧社」在微信上线，后改名「火星观剧」，是腾讯首款独立短剧产品。2025 年 6 月，微信上线名为「短剧」的官方小程序。到 2026 年 10 月，这个小程序已找不到入口，位置让给了绿泡泡。（来源：北京日报）
小鹏发布智能汽车解决方案业务

2026 巴黎国际车展期间，小鹏集团董事长兼 CEO 何小鹏作为巴黎汽车峰会唯一受邀的中国车企 CEO，发表重要演讲。何小鹏向与会的行业高管、全球媒体等，正式介绍其智能汽车解决方案业务：「XPENG AI ENGINEERING」，小鹏将面向全球合作伙伴开放智能汽车技术合作，输出覆盖整车研发、生产到售后的一站式能力。并将开放涵盖机器人、Robotaxi、飞行汽车、图灵 AI 芯片、物理世界基座模型等物理 AI 生态全领域的技术合作方案。
何小鹏表示：「开放已经成为小鹏与全球伙伴深化合作的关键词。我们不仅与合作伙伴共享技术，更与合作伙伴共同成长，全力支持合作伙伴掌握技术、开展自主创新。我们也欢迎全球合作伙伴加入，让我们互通技术、互学共进、携手前行」。（来源：新浪科技）
比亚迪欧洲建厂计划披露：法国候选
日前，比亚迪执行副总裁李柯在 2026 巴黎车展上表示，比亚迪将在欧洲大规模投资制造，比亚迪匈牙利工厂计划在今年第四季度启动大规模生产。
同时，比亚迪也将在欧洲建立第二、第三工厂。目前，法国已进入比亚迪欧洲建厂的候选名单。（来源：第一财经）
消息称 Anthropic 第三季度营收达 168 亿美元，已实现调整后盈利
10 月 15 日消息，据彭博社报道，知情人士透露，人工智能模型企业 Anthropic PBC 向潜在投资者表示，公司第三季度营收达到 168 亿美元，这家企业正继续推进上市计划。
知情人士称，开发 Claude 的 Anthropic 于当地时间周三在旧金山总部举办了推介会，向投资者说明，公司在该季度实现了调整后盈利。
知情人士表示，截至第三季度，Anthropic 已经实现正向自由现金流，调整后毛利率为 85%，调整后营业利润率超过 11%。
Anthropic 预计最早在 11 月 9 日那一周正式启动首次公开募股的路演工作，有望在感恩节前挂牌交易，预计年内完成上市。
知情人士表示，相关讨论仍在进行，时间安排仍有可能变动。（来源：IT 之家）
千问办公发布电商版，开启邀测
10 月 14 日，千问办公发布千问办公电商版，基于电商行业商家的日常工作场景进行了 AI 能力的重新设计和增强，尤其是针对跨多平台的电商经营场景，用一个 AI 入口驱动不同的电商平台，帮助商家完成 AI 时代的运营升级。
千问办公电商版已开启邀测，在千问办公中切换至「电商经营」模式即可体验。（来源：新浪科技）
国行 Apple Watch 上线睡眠呼吸暂停迹象提示功能
10 月 14 日消息，今日，苹果宣布在中国大陆推出 Apple Watch「睡眠呼吸暂停通知」功能，Apple 已获得移动睡眠呼吸暂停迹象提示软件由国家药品监督管理局（NMPA）批准的医疗器械注册证。
移动睡眠呼吸暂停迹象提示软件可以在你睡眠期间监测呼吸紊乱，并会在监测到持续性中度到重度睡眠呼吸暂停迹象时通知你。
据悉，该功能早在 2024 年便已登陆部分市场的 Apple Watch，可帮助用户识别中度至重度睡眠呼吸暂停迹象。
具体是如何识别的？苹果官方回应：基于深度学习算法及临床测试数据集构建，利用手表内置的加速感应器监测手腕细微动作以评估正常呼吸节律中断情况。
根据苹果公布的信息，支持该功能的设备包括 Apple Watch Series 9 及后续机型、Apple Watch Ultra 2 及后续机型，以及 Apple Watch SE 3。
具体操作上，将 iPhone 和手表更新至最新系统，打开 iPhone 上的健康 App，在「摘要」中找到「健康核对清单」，下滑最底部找到「移动睡眠呼吸暂停迹象提示软件」，根据指引开通即可。
需要注意的是，开通前需要确保设置过「睡眠」，并打开「通过 Apple Watch 跟踪睡眠」。
开通后，系统每 30 天会对呼吸紊乱数据进行分析。如果数据显示持续存在中度至重度睡眠呼吸暂停的迹象，用户会收到通知。需要注意的是，在为期 30 天的评估期内，必须戴着 Apple Watch 睡至少 10 晚。（来源：TechWeb）
豆包工作支持一键导入 GPT、Claude Code 技能对话，无缝切换
豆包工作正式上线数据导入同步新能力，用户可以一键把 ChatGPT、Claude Code、Trae Work 上面的技能、历史对话、工作记忆迁移过来，实现不同 AI 工具之间无缝切换。（来源：快科技）
会飞的车！特斯拉 Roadster 发布时间定档：马斯克转发预热
特斯拉官宣第二代 Roadster 将于美国时间 10 月 15 日在 SpaceX 测试基地线上直播演示，马斯克也在社交平台转发消息。
这款超跑最早于 2017 年亮相，马斯克曾提出移植 SpaceX 冷气推进技术、布置约 10 个推进器的构想，该构想可优化车辆加速表现、过弯车身姿态甚至实现短暂离地，被外界称为「会飞的跑车」。（来源：快科技）
全球首款 8K 超高清 AI 空间相机：禾赛 Kosmo One 发布，让建模像拍照一样简单
10 月 14 日现场消息，禾赛科技今日发布了「全球首款 8K 超高清 AI 空间相机」——Kosmo One，可将真实世界转化为高质量三维空间模型。
禾赛 Kosmo One 搭载一英寸 CMOS，最高拍摄分辨率可达 8K，实现 360° 无死角覆盖；15 分钟即可完成 100m² 真实空间重建，宣称「让高质量空间建模像拍照一样简单」。
禾赛 Kosmo One 可将真实世界转化为机器人训练数据，用于机器人进行物理 AI 训练，并且可用于世界模型、影视媒体、文旅文化、数字艺术等领域。
禾赛还一同发布了 Kosmo World，这是一个 AI 驱动的云平台，搭配 Kosmo One 可进行一站式 3D 内容创作与管理。（来源：IT 之家）
消息称 Nothing 将推两款智能眼镜：音频版、摄像头版，后者支持 ChatGPT
10 月 14 日消息，据消息人士 Roland Quandt 今日透露，Nothing 将推出两款智能眼镜。其中一款主打音频功能，另一款配备摄像头。

items.title: 曝高通启动全球裁员；上线 40 天，Muse 下载量突破 1000 万次；ChatGPT 上线幻灯片工具
items.summary:
DeepSeek 开源大规模云服务推理框架


10 月 20 日下午，DeepSeek 宣布，在此前开源一系列大模型、TileLang 编译工具及推理算子库的基础上，决定进一步将内部推理框架 DeepInfer 全面开源。
